Oklahoma HVACR Limited Contractor - Online Exam Prep Course

Prepare for the Oklahoma HVACR Limited Contractor licensing examination with a comprehensive Online Exam Prep Course designed to strengthen heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and refrigeration knowledge. This course provides structured preparation focused on mechanical codes, fuel gas requirements, residential load calculations, duct sizing, refrigeration systems, electrical controls, trade mathematics, and construction safety.

Designed for experienced HVACR technicians, licensed mechanical journeymen, heating and cooling specialists, and professionals pursuing contractor licensing, this course supports preparation for the Oklahoma HVACR Limited Contractor examination.

HVACR contractor examination preparation requires more than practical installation and service experience. Candidates must understand equipment operation, interpret mechanical codes, calculate heating and cooling loads, evaluate duct systems, and apply technical requirements to mechanical installations.

The Oklahoma HVACR Limited Contractor Online Exam Prep Course organizes these subjects into a focused preparation approach emphasizing technical knowledge, calculations, practical applications, and reference navigation.

The course focuses on seven important study references: the Ductulator, International Mechanical Code, 2024, International Fuel Gas Code, 2024, Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition, Manual J - Residential Load Calcs, Reprinted 2016, Eighth Full Edition, Mathematics for Plumbers and Pipefitters, 8th Edition, and Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA).

Important Course Information: Physical copies of the listed study references are not included with the online course. The Online Exam Prep Course provides structured online preparation centered on technical subjects and listed study references.

Whether you are advancing from journeyman-level HVACR work or preparing for the additional responsibilities associated with mechanical contracting, this course supports organized preparation for the technical examination.

Exam Details

The Oklahoma HVACR Contractor Limited examination evaluates technical knowledge involving heating, cooling, refrigeration, ventilation, air distribution, electrical controls, natural gas systems, and mechanical safety.

The Oklahoma Construction Industries Board oversees mechanical contractor licensing, while PSI administers the applicable examinations.

  • Examination: Oklahoma HVACR Contractor - Limited
  • Licensing Authority: Oklahoma Construction Industries Board
  • Testing Provider: PSI
  • Number of Scored Questions: 80
  • Time Allowed: 210 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%
  • Correct Answers Required: 56
  • Examination Format: Open book
  • Mechanical Code Reference: International Mechanical Code, 2024
  • Fuel Gas Code Reference: International Fuel Gas Code, 2024

The examination addresses six major technical subject areas:

  • Electrical Knowledge and Controls: 15 questions covering electrical theory, motors, AC and DC circuits, and controls.
  • Natural Gas: 12 questions involving piping materials, valves, connectors, supports, sizing, and testing.
  • Air Distribution Systems: 15 questions addressing duct design, installation, insulation, ventilation, and testing.
  • Refrigeration and Air Conditioning: 20 questions involving refrigerants, equipment, piping, system operation, and troubleshooting.
  • Heating Systems: 15 questions covering heating equipment, combustion air, venting, installation, and hydronic systems.
  • Safety: 3 questions involving workplace protection and construction hazards.

With 210 minutes available for 80 questions, candidates have approximately two minutes and 38 seconds per question. Effective preparation involves developing technical understanding while practicing efficient reference navigation.

Oklahoma mechanical contractor licensing also includes a separate Mechanical Business and Law examination. This online course focuses on the HVACR Limited Contractor trade examination and the seven listed technical references.

Open Book Test

The Oklahoma HVACR Limited Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates may consult approved examination references according to PSI testing requirements.

Open-book testing requires more than locating individual terms in reference books. Candidates must identify the mechanical subject, determine the appropriate source, interpret technical information, and apply installation requirements correctly.

The International Mechanical Code addresses mechanical equipment, ventilation, duct systems, refrigeration, and installation requirements. The International Fuel Gas Code covers gas piping, regulators, appliance connections, combustion air, and venting.

The Ductulator supports duct-sizing calculations, while Manual J addresses residential heating and cooling load calculations. Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning provides technical information about refrigeration systems and equipment operation.

Oklahoma adopted the 2024 International Mechanical Code and International Fuel Gas Code, with applicable state amendments, effective September 14, 2026.

The examination transition period runs from September 14 through December 14, 2026. During this period, affected candidates may test using either the previously adopted or newly adopted building codes.

Beginning December 15, 2026, affected examinations will use the newly adopted codes exclusively.

PSI permits approved references to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Permanent tabs are permitted, while unauthorized handwritten notes and temporary removable tabs are prohibited.

Regular practice using code indexes, equipment tables, duct-sizing tools, load calculation references, and technical formulas helps candidates develop more efficient examination preparation habits.

Licensing Steps

Oklahoma HVACR Limited Contractor licensing is administered by the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board under the state's mechanical licensing framework.

  1. Review the Contractor Classification: Understand the authorized work and equipment capacity limits associated with HVACR Limited contracting.
  2. Meet Mechanical Experience Requirements: Complete the applicable qualifying mechanical trade experience.
  3. Satisfy Journeyman Qualifications: Meet the requirements for mechanical journeyman eligibility and obtain the additional qualifying experience required for contractor licensing.
  4. Prepare for the Trade Examination: Study mechanical codes, refrigeration, heating systems, natural gas, ductwork, calculations, and safety.
  5. Prepare for Business and Law: Review the separate examination addressing contractor business and legal responsibilities.
  6. Submit the Licensing Application: Complete the required application through the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board.
  7. Receive Examination Authorization: Complete the Board's eligibility review.
  8. Complete Required Examinations: Schedule and pass the applicable examinations through PSI.
  9. Finalize Contractor Licensing: Satisfy remaining licensing, firm, insurance, and bonding requirements.

Oklahoma mechanical contractor applicants must meet the applicable journeyman qualifications plus one additional year of qualifying mechanical trade experience.

Mechanical contractors must also be permanent employees, owners, partners, or officers of the mechanical firms associated with their contractor licenses.

State Requirements

HVACR contracting in Oklahoma is regulated through state mechanical licensing laws, administrative regulations, and adopted mechanical construction codes.

The HVACR Limited Contractor classification authorizes qualified license holders to install, alter, modify, service, maintain, or repair cooling systems with capacities of 25 tons or less and heating equipment with heat input ratings of 500,000 Btu/h or less per appliance.

The classification also includes authorized sheet metal, natural gas piping, refrigeration, and related process piping work.

These capacity limitations distinguish the limited classification from the HVACR Unlimited Contractor classification.

Contractors must understand mechanical installation requirements involving equipment selection, airflow, ductwork, refrigeration, ventilation, fuel gas systems, and safety.

The International Mechanical Code and International Fuel Gas Code establish technical provisions adopted by Oklahoma with applicable amendments.

Contractor responsibilities also include maintaining applicable business licensing, insurance, bonding, and professional compliance requirements.

Reference Books

The Oklahoma HVACR Limited Contractor Online Exam Prep Course focuses on seven important technical study references:

  • Ductulator
    A practical duct-sizing calculation tool used to evaluate airflow, duct dimensions, velocity, and friction loss. It supports preparation involving air distribution design and duct sizing calculations commonly encountered in HVACR applications.
  • International Mechanical Code, 2024
    Published by the International Code Council, this code establishes requirements for mechanical equipment, heating and cooling installations, ventilation, duct systems, refrigeration, equipment access, and mechanical safety. It supports technical code interpretation and installation knowledge.
  • International Fuel Gas Code, 2024
    Addresses fuel gas piping materials, sizing, pressure regulators, valves, appliance connections, combustion air, venting, and system testing. It supports preparation involving gas-fired heating equipment and related mechanical installations.
  • Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition
    A comprehensive HVACR textbook covering refrigeration principles, refrigerants, compressors, condensers, evaporators, motors, electrical controls, heating systems, system operation, maintenance, and troubleshooting.
  • Manual J - Residential Load Calcs, Reprinted 2016, Eighth Full Edition
    An Air Conditioning Contractors of America reference addressing residential heating and cooling load calculations. It supports preparation involving building heat gains, heat losses, equipment sizing, and residential HVAC system design principles.
  • Mathematics for Plumbers and Pipefitters, 8th Edition
    A trade mathematics textbook covering measurements, fractions, decimals, conversions, geometry, area, volume, piping calculations, and practical numerical problem-solving relevant to mechanical work.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    Contains federal construction safety regulations involving personal protective equipment, electrical hazards, ladders, scaffolding, excavation, fall protection, tools, and workplace conditions.

These references support complementary preparation areas involving mechanical codes, natural gas systems, residential loads, duct calculations, refrigeration technology, mathematics, and safety.

Understanding Residential Heating and Cooling Load Calculations

Residential HVAC equipment selection requires an understanding of building heating and cooling demands.

Manual J provides methods for evaluating heat gains and heat losses associated with residential buildings.

Important considerations include building construction, insulation, windows, orientation, infiltration, and indoor design conditions.

Developing familiarity with load calculations helps candidates understand how equipment capacity relates to building requirements.

Compressors, condensers, evaporators, expansion devices, motors, relays, contactors, and thermostats influence equipment operation.

The Ductulator supports air distribution study involving duct sizing, airflow, friction loss, and duct dimensions.

The limited classification covers authorized work involving cooling systems of no more than 25 tons and heating equipment rated at no more than 500,000 Btu/h per appliance. The unlimited classification does not have those capacity restrictions.

Does Completing the Online Course Guarantee an Oklahoma HVACR Contractor License?

No. The course provides examination preparation. Applicants must pass the required examinations and satisfy the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board's licensing requirements.

Prepare for the Mississippi HVAC contractor examination with an online course designed to organize your study process around the trade knowledge, code references, calculations, and book-navigation skills needed for an open-book contractor exam. The Mississippi HVAC Contractor - Online Exam Prep Course supports experienced HVAC professionals who want a structured way to review important subjects and become more confident using the examination reference materials.

The Mississippi HVAC exam covers a broad range of heating, ventilation, air-conditioning, refrigeration, fuel-gas, ductwork, load-calculation, piping, and construction-safety topics. Studying effectively requires more than reading one general HVAC textbook. Candidates must understand how the listed references work together and learn which book is most likely to contain the answer to a particular type of question.

This online exam prep course helps candidates organize the material into manageable study areas. The preparation focuses on trade review, practice-oriented learning, reference navigation, code lookup, calculations, and test-taking structure. Candidates can use the course alongside the listed examination books to strengthen their ability to identify key terms, select the correct reference, and locate information efficiently.

Because the Mississippi HVAC contractor examination is open book, familiarity with the references is essential. Open book does not mean that candidates can search every book from beginning to end during the test. The examination requires practical trade knowledge, careful reading, efficient navigation, and the ability to apply technical information within the available testing time.

The books listed on this page are the references used to support course study and examination preparation. Books are not included with this online course unless they are purchased separately as part of another package. Candidates should have access to the correct titles and editions while completing the course so they can practice using the same materials associated with the examination.

Exam Details

Mississippi identifies Heat, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning as a tested specialty contractor classification. Its scope includes the installation, maintenance, repair, fabrication, alteration, and extension of HVAC systems. The classification also includes associated HVAC equipment, ductwork, duct cleaning, industrial air systems used for dust control, ventilation systems, and related work.

Applicants begin the licensing process by submitting the applicable contractor license application to the Mississippi State Board of Contractors. The Board reviews the application, notifies the applicant when requirements are missing, and sends eligible candidate information to PSI. Candidates cannot schedule their examinations until PSI receives their eligibility and provides registration instructions.

All Mississippi contractor applicants are required to complete the Mississippi Law and Business Management examination. A trade examination may also be required according to the classification requested. Candidates pursuing the HVAC classification should prepare for the applicable HVAC trade examination unless the Mississippi State Board of Contractors approves a trade-exam waiver under an available reciprocity provision.

The HVAC trade examination may address refrigeration principles, heating and cooling systems, HVAC equipment, controls, piping, insulation, ventilation, exhaust systems, duct construction, fuel-gas installations, liquefied petroleum gas, combustion air, chimneys, vents, load calculations, duct sizing, safety, and practical trade mathematics.

Questions may require candidates to recognize a technical principle, interpret a code provision, find information in a table, identify an installation requirement, or complete a calculation. Preparation should therefore combine subject review with active use of the listed reference materials.

The Mississippi Law and Business Management examination focuses on the responsibilities associated with operating a contracting business. Candidates should also prepare for subjects such as licensing, bidding, estimating, contracts, project management, financial management, business organization, taxes, labor responsibilities, risk management, safety, and other contractor business topics.

Open Book Test

Mississippi contractor examinations administered by PSI are open book. Candidates are responsible for bringing the references permitted for the examinations they schedule and following the current testing rules concerning book editions, markings, tabs, notes, and additional materials.

An open-book exam rewards candidates who know how the references are organized. A candidate who opens an unfamiliar book for the first time during the test may spend too much time searching for one answer. Regular practice helps build familiarity with each book’s index, table of contents, chapter structure, formulas, charts, and code arrangement.

The online course is designed to support that preparation by connecting study topics with the references where those topics are commonly addressed. When reviewing fuel-gas questions, candidates should know how to use the International Fuel Gas Code. When studying mechanical-system requirements, they should practice with the International Mechanical Code. Load calculations and duct-design questions require familiarity with the applicable ACCA manuals and calculation tools.

Effective book navigation begins with identifying the main subject of the question. Candidates should determine whether the question concerns refrigeration, mechanical code, fuel gas, LP gas, OSHA safety, duct construction, piping, residential load calculations, commercial load calculations, or duct sizing. That decision helps narrow the search to the most appropriate reference.

Candidates should review the current PSI Candidate Information Bulletin before test day. PSI determines which reference materials may enter the examination room and what types of tabs, highlighting, notes, or markings are accepted. Testing rules should be followed carefully to avoid delays or rejection of a reference at the testing center.

Licensing Steps

  1. Select the appropriate classification. Confirm that the Mississippi HVAC contractor classification matches the work the business intends to perform.
  2. Determine the applicant structure. Identify whether the application will be submitted by an individual, limited liability company, corporation, partnership, or another eligible business entity.
  3. Select the qualifying party. Designate the person who will qualify the company and complete the required examinations.
  4. Complete the contractor application. Provide the requested business, ownership, qualifying-party, financial, insurance, and supporting information.
  5. Submit the application to the Mississippi State Board of Contractors. The Board must receive and review the application before the candidate can schedule an examination.
  6. Respond to application requests. Supply missing documents, corrections, or additional information requested during the review.
  7. Receive examination eligibility. After eligibility is approved, the Board sends the candidate’s information to PSI.
  8. Register with PSI. Follow the testing provider’s instructions to schedule the required examination dates.
  9. Prepare with the online course and reference books. Review the trade subjects, practice calculations, and develop efficient reference-navigation skills.
  10. Take the required examinations. Bring acceptable identification and only the books and materials permitted under the current testing rules.
  11. Complete outstanding licensing requirements. Submit any remaining documentation needed for final application review.
  12. Receive the Board’s licensing decision. Passing the examinations does not automatically issue a license. The complete application must be reviewed and approved.

State Requirements

The Mississippi State Board of Contractors administers the contractor licensing process for the applicable HVAC classification. Candidates must apply under the classification that corresponds with the services the business intends to offer.

The Heat, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning specialty classification includes work involving HVAC system installation, maintenance, repair, fabrication, alteration, and extension. It also includes associated equipment, ductwork, duct cleaning, industrial air systems for dust control, ventilation systems, and related work.

The qualifying party must be appropriately connected to the applicant and satisfy the requirements associated with the requested classification. The application may require documentation showing the qualifying party’s role, employment, ownership, or relationship to the business.

Commercial contractor applicants may be required to submit a reviewed financial statement prepared by a certified public accountant. Other application requirements may include business registration records, tax identification information, reference letters, general liability insurance documentation, workers’ compensation information when applicable, and supporting information about the qualifying party.

Every applicant must complete the Mississippi Law and Business Management examination. The HVAC trade examination may be waived only when the Board approves an applicable reciprocity request. Reciprocity applies to the trade examination rather than the entire licensing process, so applicants must still complete the Mississippi application and satisfy the remaining requirements.

Passing an examination is one part of the contractor licensing process. A candidate should not represent the business as licensed until the Mississippi State Board of Contractors has completed its review and issued the applicable credential.

Additional local requirements may apply to HVAC work. Depending on the project and location, a contractor may need permits, inspections, registrations, insurance coverage, or approvals from a city, county, project owner, or other authority.

Reference Books

The following books support study for the Mississippi HVAC contractor trade examination. They are not included with the online course unless purchased separately.

  • Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition
    A comprehensive HVAC reference covering refrigeration principles, refrigerants, heating systems, cooling systems, equipment, controls, components, installation practices, troubleshooting concepts, and system operation.
  • Code of Federal Regulations—29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    A federal construction-safety reference covering workplace hazards, personal protective equipment, fall protection, electrical safety, tools, scaffolding, materials handling, excavation, and other construction activities.
  • International Fuel Gas Code, 2021 Edition
    A code reference addressing fuel-gas piping, appliances, equipment connections, combustion air, venting, testing, installation requirements, and safety provisions.
  • HVAC Duct Construction Standards—Metal and Flexible, 2005, 3rd Edition
    A technical standard covering the fabrication, reinforcement, support, assembly, installation, and construction of metal and flexible HVAC duct systems.
  • Manual N—Commercial Load Calculation for Small Commercial Buildings, 5th Edition
    An ACCA reference for calculating heating and cooling loads in small commercial buildings using design conditions, construction details, heat transfer, occupancy, ventilation, and internal loads.
  • International Mechanical Code, 2021 Edition
    A mechanical-code reference addressing HVAC equipment, ventilation, exhaust systems, duct systems, combustion air, appliance installation, mechanical rooms, chimneys, vents, and related requirements.
  • NFPA 58 Liquefied Petroleum Gas Code, 2020 Edition
    A code covering the storage, handling, transportation, installation, and use of liquefied petroleum gas, including containers, piping, equipment, separation requirements, and safety practices.
  • Ductulator
    A practical HVAC tool used to compare airflow, duct dimensions, friction rate, and velocity when sizing or evaluating air-distribution systems.
  • Manual D, 2016, 3rd Edition
    An ACCA residential duct-design reference covering airflow requirements, available static pressure, friction rate, fittings, equivalent length, duct sizing, balancing, and system performance.
  • Pipefitter’s Handbook
    A field-oriented reference containing piping formulas, dimensions, fitting data, measurement information, layout methods, conversion tables, and practical pipefitting calculations.
  • Manual J—Residential Load Calculations, Reprinted 2016, Eighth Full Edition
    An ACCA reference for calculating residential heating and cooling loads based on climate, insulation, construction materials, windows, doors, infiltration, orientation, occupancy, and internal heat gains.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive study plan should connect each examination subject with the reference most likely to address it. Candidates should avoid treating the books as one large collection. Dividing them into clear subject groups makes studying and navigation more manageable.

Use Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning for broad trade review involving refrigeration cycles, refrigerants, heating and cooling systems, equipment, controls, components, and HVAC operating principles.

Use the International Mechanical Code for mechanical-system requirements involving equipment installation, ventilation, exhaust, duct systems, combustion air, chimneys, and vents. Use the International Fuel Gas Code for fuel-gas piping, appliance connections, testing, combustion air, and venting. Use NFPA 58 for liquefied petroleum gas subjects.

Use the OSHA reference for questions involving construction safety and workplace practices. Use the HVAC duct construction standard for duct materials, reinforcement, joints, supports, fabrication, and installation.

Manual J supports residential load calculations, while Manual N addresses small-commercial load calculations. Manual D and the Ductulator help candidates work through duct sizing, airflow, velocity, friction rate, pressure, fittings, and system-design questions. The Pipefitter’s Handbook supports piping dimensions, fitting information, formulas, and field calculations.

Timed lookup practice should be part of every study schedule. Select a topic, identify the correct book, find the term in the index, and locate the relevant section. Record how long the search takes and repeat difficult lookups until the process becomes familiar.

Calculation practice should include reading the problem carefully, listing the known values, selecting the correct formula or procedure, checking units, completing the calculation, and reviewing whether the result is reasonable. Candidates should use the applicable manuals and tools while practicing instead of relying only on memorized formulas.

During the examination, candidates can begin with questions they recognize and return to more difficult questions after completing the easier material. When a question requires a reference search, identifying its central keyword can help determine the correct book and index term.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps Mississippi HVAC contractor candidates organize a large amount of technical material into a more focused study process. The online course supports trade review, practice-oriented preparation, reference navigation, code familiarity, and calculation practice.

The course is designed to complement the listed examination references. Candidates can follow an organized study structure while using their books to locate information, review important subjects, and practice the skills required for an open-book test.

Trade-focused preparation helps candidates connect practical HVAC experience with the terminology used in code books, technical manuals, and examination questions. This can be especially valuable when a familiar field concept is presented in a formal code or calculation format.

Reference-navigation practice helps candidates learn where information is located and how different books apply to different subjects. Repeated practice can reduce unnecessary searching and help candidates approach the exam with a clearer strategy.

1 Exam Prep also emphasizes confidence-building study structure. Breaking the material into manageable subjects can make it easier to maintain a consistent study routine, identify weak areas, and revisit difficult topics before the examination.

The course does not guarantee a passing score, examination eligibility, or licensing approval. Results depend on the candidate’s experience, preparation, understanding of the material, ability to use the references, performance on test day, and completion of all Mississippi licensing requirements.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the Mississippi HVAC online course cover?

The course supports preparation involving HVAC systems, refrigeration, mechanical code, fuel gas, LP gas, duct construction, piping, safety, load calculations, duct design, reference navigation, and test-taking structure.

Are the reference books included with the online course?

No. The listed books support course study and exam preparation but are not included with this online course unless purchased separately through another package.

Is the Mississippi HVAC contractor exam open book?

Yes. Mississippi contractor examinations administered by PSI are open book. Candidates must bring permitted references and comply with current testing-center rules.

Do I need every listed reference?

Candidates should follow the current PSI Candidate Information Bulletin for the examination they schedule. The bulletin identifies the reference materials and editions associated with the exam.

Does the course teach the HVAC trade from the beginning?

The course is designed for exam preparation and does not replace field training or practical HVAC experience. It helps experienced candidates review trade subjects and prepare to use the examination references.

Does the course include Mississippi Business and Law preparation?

This product is focused on the Mississippi HVAC contractor trade examination. Candidates should prepare separately for the required Mississippi Law and Business Management examination.

Can the HVAC trade examination be waived through reciprocity?

A trade-exam waiver may be available when the applicant satisfies an applicable reciprocity agreement and receives approval from the Mississippi State Board of Contractors. Reciprocity does not waive the Mississippi application or Law and Business Management examination.

Can I schedule the exam before submitting my application?

No. The Mississippi State Board of Contractors must receive the application and notify PSI of the candidate’s eligibility before examination scheduling is permitted.

Does completing the course guarantee a passing score?

No. Examination results depend on the candidate’s trade knowledge, study effort, reference-navigation ability, calculation skills, and performance on test day.

Does passing the exam automatically issue a contractor license?

No. Passing the required examinations is one part of the licensing process. The complete application and supporting documentation must also be reviewed and approved by the Mississippi State Board of Contractors.

Exam Details

The Oklahoma HVACR Journeyman Unlimited examination tests knowledge of the installation, maintenance, repair, fabrication, alteration, and extension of air conditioning, refrigeration, heating, and ventilating systems. The scope includes ductwork within a complete system unlimited in horsepower or tons, together with related appurtenances, piping, vessels, ducts, and insulation while employed by an HVACR contractor.

  • Exam: Oklahoma HVACR Journeyman Unlimited
  • Testing Provider: PSI
  • Number of Questions: 70
  • Time Allowed: 180 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%
  • Passing Raw Score: 49 correct answers
  • Exam Format: Open book

The examination is divided among six major content areas. Electrical Knowledge and Controls contains 15 questions. Natural Gas contains 10 questions. Air Distribution Systems contains 16 questions. Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Systems contains 16 questions. Heating Systems contains 10 questions, and Safety contains 3 questions.

Electrical Knowledge and Controls includes general electrical theory and knowledge, motors, DC circuits, AC circuits, and controls. HVACR technicians regularly work with electrical components and control systems, so candidates should be comfortable connecting basic electrical principles with HVACR equipment operation and troubleshooting.

Natural Gas includes piping valves, connectors, accessories, hangers and supports, sizing, materials, testing, installation, and assembly. Candidates should understand practical fuel gas concepts while also becoming familiar with the structure of the International Fuel Gas Code.

Air Distribution Systems covers duct definitions, sizing and design, assembly and installation, hangers and supports, duct materials and shapes, insulation, fire and smoke control, hoods and exhaust systems, testing and balancing, ventilation requirements, plans, and symbols.

Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Systems includes theory, refrigerants, equipment sizing and design, equipment and components, piping, equipment installation, system operation, troubleshooting, and maintenance. Heating Systems includes heating theory and types, combustion air, vents and chimneys, equipment sizing, heating equipment, equipment installation, hydronics and hydronic piping, system operation, troubleshooting, and maintenance.

Safety topics include personal protective equipment, safety training, employee ventilation, first aid requirements, work around toxic materials, fall protection, lockout/tagout procedures, ladders, scaffolds, and related construction safety responsibilities.

Open Book Test

The Oklahoma HVACR Journeyman Unlimited examination is an open book test. Candidates may bring approved reference materials into the examination center under PSI's reference rules.

Reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination session. Permanent tabs are permitted. Temporary tabs such as Post-it notes are not allowed, and candidates may not write in their references before or during the examination.

Open-book testing makes navigation skills especially important. With 70 questions and 180 minutes, candidates need to manage their time carefully. Searching through every book for every question can quickly consume valuable testing time.

The course supports a more organized approach. First identify the subject of the question. Then determine which reference is most likely to contain the applicable information. After selecting the reference, use the index, chapter structure, table of contents, definitions, or permanent tabs to locate the answer efficiently.

Mechanical installation, ventilation, ductwork, equipment, refrigeration-code, combustion-air, chimney, and vent questions may involve the International Mechanical Code. Fuel gas piping, materials, sizing, connectors, appliances, testing, combustion air, and venting may involve the International Fuel Gas Code.

Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning supports broader technical topics involving refrigeration theory, refrigerants, heating, air conditioning, equipment, controls, system operation, service, maintenance, and troubleshooting. Mathematics for Plumbers and Pipefitters supports trade calculations, while 29 CFR Part 1926 supports construction-safety preparation.

Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition is permitted for this examination beginning August 13, 2026.

Licensing Steps

Oklahoma mechanical journeyman licensing is administered by the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board. Candidates must satisfy the applicable licensing qualifications in addition to preparing for and passing the examination.

  1. Gain qualifying HVACR experience. Build verifiable mechanical trade experience in the HVACR category for which you are applying.
  2. Meet journeyman qualifications. Oklahoma recognizes qualifying experience and approved combinations of formal mechanical education and trade experience.
  3. Qualify for the Unlimited category. Experience used for the Unlimited classification must demonstrate work appropriate to the unrestricted HVACR scope.
  4. Submit the mechanical license application. Apply through the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board for the HVACR Unlimited Journeyman classification.
  5. Receive approval to test. The state reviews the application and determines examination eligibility.
  6. Schedule the PSI examination. Approved applicants complete the testing-provider scheduling process.
  7. Prepare for the open-book examination. Study the technical categories while practicing use of the approved references.
  8. Complete the licensing process. After meeting examination requirements, follow the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board process for obtaining and maintaining the journeyman license.

Exam preparation should be coordinated with the licensing process so candidates understand both the technical knowledge being tested and the scope of the credential they are pursuing.

State Requirements

The Oklahoma HVACR Unlimited Journeyman classification authorizes the licensee to install, alter, modify, service, maintain, or repair qualifying cooling products, systems, or equipment, including process piping, without the 25-ton cooling-capacity restriction that applies to the HVACR Limited Journeyman classification.

The Unlimited classification also covers heating equipment, including process piping, without the 500,000 Btu/h per-appliance limitation associated with the Limited classification.

Qualifying sheet metal, natural gas piping, and refrigeration work are also included within the scope of the HVACR Unlimited Journeyman license.

Mechanical journeyman applicants must satisfy Oklahoma's applicable experience or education-and-experience requirements. The Unlimited category requires experience appropriate to work beyond the capacity limitations of the HVACR Limited classification.

The journeyman credential operates within Oklahoma's mechanical licensing structure, and a journeyman performs licensed work while working for the applicable mechanical contractor. Candidates should understand the difference between journeyman and contractor licensing when planning their career path.

A strong Oklahoma HVACR Journeyman Unlimited study plan should balance technical knowledge with reference navigation. The exam moves across multiple HVACR subjects, so preparation should not focus on only one code book or one area of field experience.

Electrical Knowledge and Controls accounts for 15 questions. Review electrical theory, motors, AC and DC circuits, and HVACR control concepts. Open-book testing does not eliminate the need to study. HVAC and refrigeration references contain extensive technical information, and attempting to locate every answer in unfamiliar books during the examination can take valuable time.

The books included with The 1 Package are highlighted and tabbed to provide an organized starting point. Highlighting helps identify important material, while tabs can make major subject areas and commonly used sections easier to reach during preparation.

Use the books regularly while working through the course. When reviewing mechanical code requirements, practice using the International Mechanical Code. When studying refrigeration systems, locate related information in the refrigeration references. When reviewing safety topics, work directly with OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926.

Reference familiarity comes from repetition. Learn how each book is structured, where important chapters are located, and how to use indexes and tables of contents. When working through practice questions, identify the subject first and then choose the book most likely to contain the information.

Instead of randomly searching across every reference, develop a repeatable system: identify the topic, choose the book, locate the applicable section, read the information carefully, and then answer the question.

Licensing Steps

Tennessee contractor licensing is administered by the Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors. The CMC-C classification is identified as the HVAC/Refrigeration Contractor classification. Tennessee also requires contractor applicants pursuing tested classifications to complete applicable examination and licensing requirements. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

  1. Determine the correct contractor classification. Make sure the Tennessee CMC-C HVAC/Refrigeration Contractor classification corresponds with the work your business intends to perform.
  2. Establish your business structure. The 1 Package includes Business Formation assistance for an LLC or corporation.
  3. Prepare for the required examinations. Use the course and highlighted and tabbed references to develop trade knowledge, business knowledge, and open-book navigation skills.
  4. Complete the applicable contractor application. Provide the required business, ownership, qualifying-agent, financial, and other application information.
  5. Complete the applicable examinations. Candidates pursuing a tested contractor classification complete the trade examination and applicable Business and Law examination requirements.
  6. Provide required licensing documentation. Complete the supporting documentation requirements associated with the contractor application.
  7. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Examination completion is one part of the licensing process. The Board determines whether the applicant has satisfied the requirements necessary for license issuance.

Application Service is included with The 1 Package to provide support while you work through the contractor licensing process.

State Requirements

Tennessee contractor licensing requirements depend on the classification, business entity, qualifying agent, monetary limit, and individual application. The Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors administers the licensing process and determines whether an applicant meets the requirements for the requested license. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}

The qualifying agent is the individual who satisfies the applicable examination requirement for the business seeking the contractor license. The qualifying agent may be associated with the entity according to the requirements established for Tennessee contractor applicants.

Tennessee contractor applications also involve financial information. The Board uses financial information as part of determining the monetary limit associated with a contractor license. Applicants should make sure that business, financial, ownership, and qualifying-agent information is completed accurately. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

Passing the CMC-C exam does not by itself issue a Tennessee contractor license. The examination is one component of the overall licensing process. Applicants must complete all applicable Board requirements before receiving the requested license and classification.

Exam Details

The Virginia Master HVAC credential is an individual tradesman license regulated through the Virginia Board for Contractors. Candidates must meet the applicable qualification requirements and receive approval before sitting for the examination.

Master HVAC preparation should include a broad range of technical subjects. Candidates may need to work with mechanical-system requirements, refrigeration principles, heating systems, air conditioning, ventilation, duct systems, electrical controls, troubleshooting, combustion air, oil-burning equipment, and Virginia regulatory requirements.

At the Master level, candidates should understand not only how HVAC systems operate but also how applicable code requirements affect installation, maintenance, and professional practice. Study should combine field knowledge with direct use of the technical references.

The International Mechanical Code, 2021 is an important reference for mechanical-system requirements. Candidates should become familiar with chapters covering equipment, ventilation, exhaust, ducts, combustion air, chimneys and vents, and other mechanical topics.

Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition supports broader HVAC trade preparation. NFPA 31 adds focused material involving oil-burning equipment. Candidates should understand where to find requirements related to oil-fired equipment installation, fuel systems, venting, and safety.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Master HVAC examination is open book. Candidates should prepare by working directly with their permitted references and becoming familiar with how each book is organized.

A Virginia licensing or professional-requirement question may lead to the Virginia Board for Contractors, Individual License and Certification Regulations. Mechanical-system questions may require the International Mechanical Code, 2021. Oil-fired equipment questions may require NFPA 31, while broader refrigeration, air conditioning, heating, electrical, and troubleshooting topics may be found in Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning.

The highlighted and tabbed preparation in this package helps candidates identify important sections more quickly. Highlighting can draw attention to key material, while tabs make it easier to return to major chapters and frequently used subjects.

Licensing Steps

The Virginia Master HVAC credential is an individual tradesman license. Candidates must satisfy the applicable Board requirements before the license can be issued.

  1. Review the Master HVAC qualification requirements. Determine which education, experience, or existing-license pathway applies to your background.
  2. Document the required qualifications. Applicants must provide the information requested by the Virginia Board for Contractors to establish eligibility.
  3. Submit the applicable application. The Board reviews the application and supporting information before examination approval is granted.
  4. Receive approval to test. Candidates must obtain the required approval before scheduling the Master HVAC examination.
  5. Schedule the examination. After approval, candidates can proceed with the applicable examination registration process.
  6. Prepare with the technical references. Study the Virginia regulations, International Mechanical Code, NFPA 31, and Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning while practicing reference navigation.
  7. Complete the required examination. Candidates must satisfy the applicable Master-level examination requirement.
  8. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Any outstanding Board requirements must be completed before the individual license is issued.

Candidates who intend to use the Master HVAC credential in connection with a contracting business should remember that the individual tradesman license and the Virginia contractor business license are separate credentials. The business must independently satisfy the contractor licensing requirements that apply to its class and classification or specialty.

State Requirements

The Virginia Board for Contractors regulates individual HVAC tradesmen as well as contractor businesses. A Master HVAC license is issued to an individual and reflects satisfaction of the applicable qualification and examination requirements for that trade.

A contractor business license is issued separately. Virginia contractor businesses may hold Class A, Class B, or Class C licenses and must also have the appropriate classification or specialty for the work the business performs.

For contractor businesses performing HVAC work, the appropriately qualified individual must meet the current Virginia requirements associated with the HVAC classification or specialty. Holding the Master HVAC credential can be an important part of that qualification structure, but it does not replace the business licensing process.

Virginia also imposes renewal and continuing-education requirements on individual tradesmen. Candidates preparing for initial licensure should distinguish between exam preparation and continuing education used for license renewal. This highlighted and tabbed book package is intended for examination preparation and does not replace Board-approved continuing education.

Virginia regulatory requirements can address qualifications, professional responsibilities, renewal, reinstatement, and other licensing matters. This package brings together the primary regulatory, mechanical code, oil-burning equipment, and HVAC technical references associated with preparation for the Virginia Journeyman HVAC examination.

The Virginia Journeyman Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning credential is an individual tradesman license regulated by the Virginia Board for Contractors through the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation. Candidates pursuing this license need a working understanding of heating, ventilation, air conditioning, refrigeration, duct systems, boilers, hydronic systems, controls, fuel-oil equipment, combustion air, and applicable Virginia regulations.

The examination covers a wide range of HVAC subjects, making reference familiarity especially important. Candidates may need to move between mechanical code provisions, technical HVAC information, fuel-oil requirements, and Virginia regulatory material. Because the examination is open book, learning where information is located can be an important part of an effective preparation strategy.

This Complete Highlighted & Tabbed Book Package is intended to help candidates work directly with the references throughout their preparation. Highlighting and tabbing can make major sections easier to identify while studying and can help candidates become more familiar with the structure of the books before exam day.

Please allow up to 15 business days for highlighted and tabbed book package orders.

What You Get

  • Virginia Board for Contractors, Individual License and Certification Regulations: Virginia regulatory material supporting preparation for individual tradesman licensing questions.
  • International Mechanical Code, 2021: Mechanical code reference covering HVAC systems, ventilation, duct systems, boilers, combustion air, refrigeration, exhaust systems, and related mechanical requirements.
  • NFPA 31: Standard for the Installation of Oil-Burning Equipment, 2011: Technical reference focused on oil-burning equipment, fuel-oil piping, storage, installation, and safety requirements.
  • Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition: Comprehensive HVAC technical reference covering heating, cooling, refrigeration, controls, equipment, electrical concepts, troubleshooting, and system operation.
  • Highlighted & Tabbed Preparation: The books are prepared with highlighting and tabs to support faster reference navigation during study and open-book exam preparation.
  • Order Preparation: Please allow up to 15 business days for highlighted and tabbed book package orders.

Exam Details

The Virginia Journeyman HVAC examination is administered by PSI for the Virginia Board for Contractors. Candidates must receive approval from the Board before scheduling the examination.

The current Journeyman/Master HVAC examination portion contains 85 items. A Journeyman candidate must answer 60 questions correctly to meet the Journeyman passing requirement. Candidates receive 210 minutes to complete the examination.

The examination combines Virginia tradesman regulations with technical HVAC knowledge. The current content areas include:

  • Standards of Practice: 3 items.
  • Standards of Conduct: 2 items.
  • Renewal and Reinstatement: 2 items.
  • Definitions: 1 item.
  • Qualification for Licensure: 1 item.
  • Revocation of Licensure: 1 item.
  • Warm Air Heating: 8 items.
  • Ventilation Systems: 8 items.
  • Air Conditioning Systems: 8 items.
  • Duct Systems: 6 items.
  • Chimneys, Flues, and Vents: 6 items.
  • Boilers: 5 items.
  • Hot Water Piping: 4 items.
  • Combustion Air: 4 items.
  • Controls and Low Voltage: 4 items.
  • Fuel Oil Piping and Storage: 3 items.
  • Insulation: 3 items.
  • Commercial Kitchen Venting: 5 items.
  • Refrigerants: 3 items.
  • Refrigerant Piping: 3 items.
  • Chilled and Condenser Water Piping: 3 items.
  • Firestopping and Penetration Inspection: 2 items.

Warm-air heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems account for a substantial share of the examination. Candidates should also prepare for ductwork, venting, boilers, hydronic piping, controls, combustion air, refrigeration, commercial kitchen ventilation, and fuel-oil installations.

The regulatory portion should be included in the study plan as well. Questions can address professional standards, conduct, license qualifications, definitions, renewal and reinstatement, and disciplinary provisions affecting Virginia tradesmen.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Journeyman HVAC examination is an open book test. Candidates may bring qualifying references into the examination subject to current PSI rules governing reference materials.

Reference books may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination when prepared in accordance with testing rules. Permanent tabs may be used for reference navigation, while removable tabs are not permitted. Candidates should also follow PSI requirements regarding handwritten notes and other markings in examination references.

The open-book format makes familiarity with the books an important preparation skill. Candidates receive 210 minutes for 85 questions, so spending several minutes searching through every reference for each question can make time management difficult.

A highlighted and tabbed reference package can support a more organized study routine by making major subjects easier to locate. Candidates should still spend time using the books before exam day. Tabs are most useful when the candidate knows what each tab represents and understands which reference is most appropriate for the question.

For example, questions involving ventilation, ducts, boilers, mechanical refrigeration, combustion air, and related code requirements may point toward the International Mechanical Code. Fuel-oil questions may require NFPA 31. Broader HVAC technical concepts may be supported by Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning. Virginia licensing and regulatory questions may direct the candidate to the Individual License and Certification Regulations.

Practicing this type of reference selection can make open-book preparation more efficient and help candidates develop a repeatable strategy for locating information.

Licensing Steps

Virginia Journeyman HVAC licensing is an individual tradesman licensing process. Applicants must satisfy the applicable Virginia Board for Contractors requirements before receiving examination approval.

  1. Determine that Journeyman HVAC is the appropriate license. Virginia regulates HVAC as an individual tradesman designation in addition to separate contractor business licensing requirements.
  2. Review the qualification pathways. Virginia recognizes combinations of practical HVAC experience, formal vocational training, related education, apprenticeship completion, and other qualifying routes.
  3. Document practical trade experience. Applicants must provide the required evidence of HVAC experience for the qualification pathway being used.
  4. Document education or training when applicable. Candidates using formal vocational training, technical education, or related college education must provide supporting documentation.
  5. Submit the applicable tradesman application. The Virginia Board for Contractors reviews the applicant’s qualifications.
  6. Receive examination approval. Pre-approval from the Board is required before the candidate may sit for the examination.
  7. Prepare for the Journeyman HVAC exam. Study both technical HVAC topics and Virginia regulatory requirements using the applicable references.
  8. Schedule the examination with PSI. After Board approval, candidates follow PSI procedures for examination registration and scheduling.
  9. Complete the Journeyman HVAC examination. Candidates must meet the applicable Journeyman passing requirement.
  10. Complete the licensing process. Licensure is handled through the Virginia Board for Contractors after the applicable requirements have been met.

State Requirements

Virginia provides multiple pathways for applicants seeking Journeyman HVAC licensure. One pathway allows applicants with four years of practical experience and 240 hours of formal vocational training in the trade to qualify.

Other pathways include five years of practical experience with 160 hours of formal vocational training, six years of practical experience with 80 hours of formal vocational training, or seven years of practical experience with 40 hours of formal vocational training.

Candidates with qualifying postsecondary education may use different combinations. An applicant with an associate degree or certificate of completion from at least a two-year tradesman-related program may qualify with two years of practical experience in the trade.

An applicant with a bachelor’s degree in an engineering curriculum related to the trade may qualify with one year of practical experience. Virginia also provides an experience-based pathway for applicants with eight years of practical experience when the required experience documentation is provided.

Approved apprenticeship completion may also affect examination requirements under Virginia regulations. Applicants should use the qualification path that accurately reflects their training, education, apprenticeship, and work experience.

Once licensed, Virginia Journeyman HVAC tradesmen are subject to continuing education requirements for renewal. HVAC tradesmen must complete three hours of Board-approved HVAC continuing education as required for license renewal. The education must relate to the applicable mechanical code and must be completed through a Board-approved provider.

  • International Mechanical Code, 2021

Virginia requires Residential HVAC Tradesman applicants to be at least 18 years old and to meet one of the approved experience and education pathways for examination qualification.

The current residential tradesman application provides several combinations of practical trade experience and formal vocational training. Applicants may qualify with two years of practical experience and 160 hours of formal vocational training, three years of practical experience and 120 hours of formal vocational training, four years of practical experience and 80 hours of formal vocational training, or five years of practical experience and 40 hours of formal vocational training.

Applicants may also qualify with six or more years of practical experience in the trade without using one of the listed vocational-training combinations. Required experience must be documented through the applicable Virginia experience-verification process.

Virginia also provides a pathway for individuals currently licensed or certified as a Residential Tradesman by an appropriate governing body outside the Commonwealth. Applicants using that pathway must provide the applicable licensing documentation required by the Board.

The Residential HVAC Tradesman license is designed specifically for residential work. Virginia introduced residential HVAC and residential plumbing tradesman licenses as additional pathways for individuals working in residential structures. Virginia's current application also states that individuals performing work above the threshold that requires contractor business licensing must address Virginia contractor licensing separately. The individual tradesman credential and the contractor business license serve different regulatory purposes.

Exam Details

The Mississippi Residential HVAC contractor examination evaluates knowledge associated with residential heating, ventilation, air conditioning, refrigeration, mechanical systems, fuel-gas installations, duct systems, load calculations, oil-burning equipment, and construction safety.

Candidates should combine practical HVAC experience with repeated use of the listed references. Examination questions may require direct code lookup, interpretation of a table, use of a formula, review of equipment requirements, or application of technical knowledge to a residential heating or cooling condition.

Manual J—Residential Load Calculations, Reprinted 2016, Eighth Full Edition, supports preparation involving residential heating and cooling load calculations. Proper load calculation helps determine the amount of heating or cooling required for the building rather than relying only on square footage or the size of existing equipment.

Load-calculation preparation may involve indoor and outdoor design conditions, building orientation, insulation, windows, doors, infiltration, ventilation, walls, ceilings, floors, duct gains, duct losses, sensible heat, latent heat, and room-by-room loads.

Candidates should understand how climate conditions, glazing, insulation levels, air leakage, occupancy, duct location, and building orientation can affect the calculated load. Accurate inputs are essential because incorrect assumptions can change the result.

The International Mechanical Code, 2021, is a primary code reference in this package. It supports preparation involving mechanical-system installation, ventilation, exhaust, duct systems, combustion air, appliances, equipment clearances, access, piping, chimneys, vents, refrigeration systems, and related safeguards.

Mechanical-code questions may involve equipment location, access, clearances, condensate disposal, ventilation, exhaust systems, duct construction, air distribution, appliance installation, combustion air, venting, refrigeration machinery, or system protection.

Candidates should become familiar with the organization of the International Mechanical Code and practice moving between chapters, definitions, tables, exceptions, referenced standards, and the index. Some questions may require several connected provisions rather than one isolated section.

The Ductulator supports practical airflow and duct-sizing work. Candidates can use it to review relationships between airflow, duct dimensions, velocity, friction loss, and equivalent duct sizes.

Duct-sizing questions may require candidates to identify a required airflow, select a friction rate, evaluate a duct size, or compare round and rectangular duct dimensions. Efficient use of the Ductulator requires repeated hands-on practice before examination day.

HVAC Duct Construction Standards—Metal and Flexible, 2005, 3rd Edition, supports preparation involving duct materials, construction classifications, reinforcement, joints, seams, supports, hangers, fittings, flexible duct, and installation practices.

Residential duct systems must be constructed and supported to maintain airflow, limit leakage, resist damage, and remain serviceable. Candidates should understand how duct size, pressure, material, reinforcement, connection methods, and installation conditions affect construction requirements.

Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition, supports broad technical review of refrigeration cycles, air-conditioning systems, heating systems, electrical components, controls, refrigerants, compressors, condensers, evaporators, metering devices, service procedures, troubleshooting, and equipment operation.

Refrigeration questions may involve heat transfer, pressure-temperature relationships, superheat, subcooling, system components, refrigerant flow, charging, recovery, evacuation, leak detection, or system performance.

Air-conditioning preparation may involve comfort conditions, sensible heat, latent heat, airflow, humidity, filters, blowers, coils, condensate, controls, and equipment operation.

Heating topics may involve electric heat, heat pumps, furnaces, combustion, burners, heat exchangers, controls, venting, airflow, and safety devices. Candidates should understand how the major components operate together as a complete system.

The International Fuel Gas Code, 2021, supports preparation involving fuel-gas piping, appliance installation, combustion air, venting, chimneys, regulators, pressure, shutoff valves, sizing, testing, and safety requirements.

Fuel-gas questions may require candidates to size piping, identify acceptable materials, review appliance connections, determine combustion-air requirements, evaluate venting arrangements, or locate required clearances and safeguards.

Candidates should practice using the fuel-gas code tables and understand the information needed before selecting a pipe size. Gas type, developed length, connected load, pressure, allowable pressure drop, and table conditions can affect the result.

Residential Oil Burners, 3rd Edition, supports preparation involving oil-fired heating equipment, fuel delivery, burners, nozzles, combustion, ignition, controls, draft, venting, maintenance, adjustment, and troubleshooting.

Oil-burner questions may involve fuel supply, pump pressure, nozzle selection, combustion air, ignition, flame characteristics, draft, safety controls, cleaning, testing, or service procedures.

The Code of Federal Regulations, 29 CFR Part 1926, supports preparation involving federal construction-safety requirements. Residential HVAC contractors may need to review electrical hazards, ladders, scaffolds, personal protective equipment, tools, material handling, housekeeping, and general jobsite responsibilities.

HVAC work may involve rooftops, attics, crawl spaces, ladders, sharp sheet metal, electrical systems, pressurized equipment, combustion appliances, refrigerants, and heavy components. Candidates should connect written safety requirements with practical field conditions.

The eight references function as a coordinated technical library. A single residential HVAC question may involve a mechanical-code provision, a load calculation, duct sizing, fuel-gas requirements, refrigeration knowledge, and a safety responsibility.

Open Book Test

The Mississippi Residential HVAC contractor examination is open book. Candidates may use permitted references during the examination, subject to current testing rules for approved titles, editions, highlighting, tabs, notes, markings, and supplemental materials.

An open-book format still requires detailed preparation. Having the correct books available does not help when a candidate cannot identify the proper reference, locate an effective search term, interpret a technical table, or complete a calculation within the available testing time.

Candidates should learn the purpose of each reference before examination day. Questions involving equipment installation, ventilation, exhaust, duct systems, appliance access, clearances, condensate, mechanical rooms, combustion air, or refrigeration-system requirements may lead to the International Mechanical Code.

Questions involving residential heating and cooling loads may require Manual J. Candidates should practice identifying the building information needed for a load calculation and locating the correct procedures, tables, and worksheets.

Questions involving airflow, duct dimensions, velocity, or friction loss may require the Ductulator. Duct-construction questions may lead to HVAC Duct Construction Standards—Metal and Flexible.

Technical questions involving refrigeration, air conditioning, heat pumps, furnaces, electrical components, controls, system operation, charging, service, or troubleshooting may lead to Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning.

Questions involving gas piping, appliance connections, combustion air, venting, shutoff valves, regulators, testing, or fuel-gas sizing may require the International Fuel Gas Code.

Questions involving oil-fired equipment, burner components, nozzles, combustion, ignition, draft, controls, or service procedures may require Residential Oil Burners.

Questions involving ladders, scaffolds, electrical hazards, personal protective equipment, tools, housekeeping, or construction-safety responsibilities may require 29 CFR Part 1926.

Search terminology is important. A gas-piping question may involve developed length, connected load, pressure, allowable pressure drop, appliance demand, or pipe-sizing tables.

A duct question may involve airflow, velocity, friction rate, equivalent diameter, static pressure, fittings, reinforcement, supports, or flexible duct.

A refrigeration question may involve superheat, subcooling, evaporator, condenser, compressor, metering device, saturation temperature, pressure, or refrigerant flow.

Candidates should read the surrounding material rather than stopping at the first matching phrase. Definitions, exceptions, table notes, installation conditions, and referenced sections can change how a requirement applies.

  1. Confirm the appropriate classification. Determine that the Mississippi Residential HVAC classification matches the heating, ventilation, air-conditioning, or mechanical services the business intends to provide.
  2. Select the qualifying party. Identify the person who will qualify the business and complete the required examinations.
  3. Document HVAC experience. Organize project information involving installation, service, refrigeration, duct systems, heating equipment, fuel-gas work, supervision, or project management.
  4. Choose the applicant structure. Determine whether the application will be submitted by an individual, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, or another accepted business entity.
  5. Prepare the contractor application. Gather the requested business, ownership, qualifying-party, experience, financial, insurance, reference, and supporting information.
  6. Submit the application. Send the completed filing to the Mississippi State Board of Contractors for review.
  7. Respond to application requests. Provide missing documents, corrections, explanations, or additional information requested during the review process.
  8. Receive examination eligibility. Follow the registration and scheduling instructions after authorization to test is issued.
  9. Schedule the required examinations. Select an available examination date and approved testing location.
  10. Obtain the reference books. Secure the correct titles and editions needed for examination preparation.
  11. Prepare the references. Add only highlighting, tabs, notes, or markings permitted under current testing rules.

  15. Take the required examinations. Bring acceptable identification and only the references and materials permitted under current testing rules.
  16. Complete outstanding requirements. Submit any remaining records, corrections, or supporting documents requested during final review.
  17. Receive licensing approval. Passing the examinations does not automatically issue a contractor license. The complete application and supporting documentation must also be approved.
  18. Maintain the license. After issuance, the contractor is responsible for renewals, insurance, permits, business records, taxes, safety obligations, and ongoing compliance.

The Mississippi State Board of Contractors administers the applicable contractor licensing process. Applicants should select the classification that accurately reflects the residential HVAC or mechanical work their business intends to perform.

The qualifying party must have a relationship with the applicant that satisfies the applicable requirements. Depending on the business structure, the qualifying party may be an owner, officer, executive staff member, or responsible managing employee.

The contractor application may require business-registration information, ownership records, qualifying-party documentation, detailed HVAC experience, references, financial information, insurance records, and other supporting materials.

Application information should be complete and consistent across company filings, ownership records, experience documents, and supporting materials. Missing or conflicting information can affect the review process.

Passing the required examinations is one part of contractor licensing. Applicants must also satisfy the application, documentation, experience, financial, insurance, and final approval requirements.

Residential HVAC contractors may also be responsible for local permits, inspections, adopted mechanical and fuel-gas codes, utility requirements, employee safety, insurance, tax registrations, and project-specific approvals.

Local requirements can vary by project location. Contractors should confirm applicable permitting, inspection, code, fuel-gas, electrical, and utility requirements before beginning regulated work.
