Exam Details

The Oklahoma HVACR Contractor Limited technical examination tests knowledge of the installation, maintenance, repair, fabrication, alteration, and extension of air conditioning, refrigeration, heating, and ventilation systems, including ductwork within a complete system subject to the Limited classification limits.

The current technical examination contains 80 scored questions with 210 minutes allowed. The passing requirement is 70%, equal to 56 correct answers.

Electrical Knowledge and Controls contains 15 questions. Topics include general electrical theory, motors, DC circuits, AC circuits, and controls. Candidates should understand how electrical systems and controls interact with HVAC/R equipment and how electrical problems can affect operation and troubleshooting.

Natural Gas contains 12 questions. Topics include piping valves, connectors, accessories, hangers and supports, sizing, materials, and testing. Candidates should become comfortable navigating the International Fuel Gas Code for gas-system requirements.

Air Distribution Systems contains 15 questions. Subjects include duct definitions, sizing and design, duct assembly and installation, hangers and supports, materials and shapes, insulation, fire and smoke control, hoods and exhaust systems, testing and balancing, ventilation requirements, plans, and symbols.

Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Systems is the largest category with 20 questions. Preparation should include refrigeration theory, refrigerants, equipment sizing and design, equipment and components, piping, equipment installation, system operation, troubleshooting, and maintenance.

Heating Systems contains 15 questions. Topics include heating theory, system types, combustion air, vents and chimneys, equipment sizing, heating equipment, installation, troubleshooting, maintenance, hydronics, and hydronic piping.

Safety contains three questions. Candidates should review personal protective equipment, safety training, ventilation, first-aid requirements, hazardous materials, fall protection, lockout/tagout, ladders, scaffolds, and related construction safety subjects.

The separate Mechanical Business and Law examination contains 50 scored questions and allows 120 minutes. Its current content areas include 10 Bidding and Estimating questions, seven Project Management and Supervision questions, five Contracts questions, eight Financial questions, five Labor and Personnel questions, four Risk Management questions, five Payroll and Payroll Taxes questions, and six Licensing Requirements questions.

Open Book Test

The Oklahoma HVACR Contractor Limited technical examination is an open-book test. The Mechanical Business and Law examination is also open book.

The technical examination reference list includes the ACCA Ductulator, International Mechanical Code, 2018 with Oklahoma revisions, International Fuel Gas Code, 2018 with Oklahoma revisions, Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, Manual J, Mathematics for Plumbers and Pipefitters, and OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926.

Code questions are based on the editions specifically identified for the examination. Candidates preparing for code-based questions should therefore become comfortable with the 2018 International Mechanical Code and 2018 International Fuel Gas Code with applicable Oklahoma revisions.

Current PSI rules permit later editions of approved non-code references. The 22nd Edition of Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning listed for this training is a later edition of the applicable non-code HVAC/R reference.

Approved references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Temporary tabs such as Post-it notes are not allowed.

References may not contain written notes before or during the examination. Candidates may not bring additional loose papers into the testing room with approved references.

A silent, non-printing, non-programmable calculator meeting the testing requirements may be used. Candidates benefit from practicing reference searches before the exam rather than relying on unfamiliar books for the first time at the testing center.

Licensing Steps

  1. Gain qualifying HVAC/R experience. Build verifiable mechanical trade experience while working within Oklahoma’s mechanical licensing structure.
  2. Meet the underlying journeyman qualifications. Mechanical Contractor applicants must satisfy the applicable journeyman-level qualification requirements.
  3. Complete additional contractor experience. Oklahoma contractor applicants must meet the journeyman requirements plus the additional qualifying mechanical experience required for contractor licensing.
  4. Maintain supporting documentation. Keep employment records, apprentice information, licensing history, qualifying educational records, and other documentation used to establish eligibility.
  5. Submit the Mechanical Contractor application. Apply to the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board for the HVAC/R Limited Contractor classification.
  6. Receive examination authorization. The Construction Industries Board determines eligibility before examination scheduling.
  7. Schedule the required examinations through PSI. Approved candidates arrange their testing appointments after receiving authorization.
  8. Prepare for the HVACR Contractor Limited technical exam. Review refrigeration, electrical controls, air distribution, natural gas, heating systems, load calculations, duct sizing, trade mathematics, and safety.
  9. Prepare for Mechanical Business and Law. Study bidding, estimating, project management, contracts, financial management, personnel, risk management, payroll, Oklahoma licensing requirements, liens, and contractor regulations.
  10. Complete the required examinations. Meet the passing requirements for the technical and Mechanical Business and Law examinations.
  11. Complete active contractor requirements. Provide the bond and commercial general liability insurance documentation required by the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board.
  12. Maintain contractor compliance. Keep licensing, insurance, bond, continuing education, and other applicable contractor requirements current.

State Requirements

The Oklahoma Construction Industries Board regulates mechanical licensing, including the HVAC/R Limited Contractor classification.

An HVAC/R Limited Contractor may perform qualifying installation, alteration, modification, service, maintenance, and repair of cooling products, systems, and equipment, including process piping, with a cooling capacity of no more than 25 tons.

The classification also covers heating equipment and associated process piping with a heat input of no more than 500,000 Btu/h per appliance. Sheet metal, natural gas piping, and refrigeration are also included within the authorized Limited scope.

These limits distinguish HVAC/R Limited licensing from the HVAC/R Unlimited classification. Work beyond the Limited capacity thresholds requires the appropriate Unlimited licensing.

Oklahoma Mechanical Contractor applicants must meet the applicable journeyman-level qualifications and the additional contractor experience requirement established by the state.

A Mechanical Contractor must be a permanent employee, owner, partner, or officer of the mechanical firm for which the individual serves as licensed contractor.

After successfully completing the required examinations, a contractor license remains inactive until applicable bond and insurance requirements are completed. An active Oklahoma Mechanical Contractor must maintain a $5,000 corporate surety bond payable to the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board.

An active Mechanical Contractor must also maintain at least $50,000 in commercial general liability insurance. The individual license holder must be identified on the insurance certificate, and the Construction Industries Board must be listed as certificate holder.

Oklahoma mechanical journeymen and contractors currently complete six hours of approved continuing education every 36 months. Contractors must also keep required license information, insurance, and active status current while engaging in mechanical contracting.

The license authorizes qualifying contractors to install, alter, modify, service, maintain, or repair cooling products, systems, and equipment, including process piping; heating equipment and associated process piping; sheet metal; natural gas piping; and refrigeration systems.

Exam Details

The Oklahoma HVACR Contractor Unlimited examination is administered by PSI after the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board determines that an applicant meets the qualifications to proceed with testing.

  • Exam: Oklahoma HVACR Contractor Unlimited
  • Number of Questions: 90
  • Passing Score: 70%
  • Passing Raw Score: 63 correct answers
  • Time Allowed: 240 minutes
  • Testing Provider: PSI

The technical examination covers six major subject categories:

  • Electrical Knowledge and Controls: 15 questions
  • Natural Gas: 12 questions
  • Air Distribution Systems: 25 questions
  • Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Systems: 20 questions
  • Heating Systems: 15 questions
  • Safety: 3 questions

Air Distribution Systems is the largest portion of the examination with 25 questions. This area can include duct definitions, sizing and design, assembly and installation, hangers and supports, duct materials and shapes, insulation, fire and smoke control, hoods and exhaust systems, testing and balancing, ventilation requirements, and plans and symbols.

Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Systems account for another 20 questions. Candidates should prepare for refrigeration theory, refrigerants, equipment sizing and design, equipment and components, piping, installation, system operation, troubleshooting, and maintenance.

Heating Systems account for 15 questions and include heating theory, system types, combustion air, vents and chimneys, equipment sizing, equipment installation, operation, troubleshooting, maintenance, and hydronic systems and piping. Electrical Knowledge and Controls also contains 15 questions, including electrical theory, motors, DC circuits, AC circuits, and controls.

With 90 questions and 240 minutes available, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes and forty seconds per question. Efficient use of the permitted references can be particularly important for calculations, equipment-sizing questions, duct problems, electrical questions, and detailed code requirements.

Mechanical contractor candidates also prepare for the Oklahoma Mechanical Business and Law examination. That examination contains 50 questions, requires a 70% passing score with 35 correct answers, and allows 120 minutes.

Open Book Test

The Oklahoma HVACR Contractor Unlimited examination is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing permitted reference materials to the examination center and complying with PSI's rules concerning those references.

The current examination reference list includes the ACCA Ductulator, International Mechanical Code, 2024 edition with Oklahoma revisions, International Fuel Gas Code, 2024 edition with Oklahoma revisions, Manual N - Load Calculation for Small Commercial Buildings, Fifth Edition, Mathematics for Plumbers and Pipefitters, 8th Edition, and Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA) with applicable amendments.

Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning is also used for examination preparation. PSI's current transition schedule permits the 22nd edition beginning August 13, 2026. The 20th and 21st editions are accepted under the current transition rules, with the 20th edition scheduled to be discontinued as an allowed reference beginning November 1, 2026.

Approved reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted for indexing. Temporary tabs such as Post-it notes are not allowed. Candidate-added writing is not permitted in the references before or during the examination session.

For an open-book HVACR examination, simply having the books available is not enough. Candidates should repeatedly practice choosing the appropriate reference, locating the relevant section or table, interpreting the information, and applying it to the question being asked.

Licensing Steps

The Oklahoma Construction Industries Board regulates mechanical contractor licensing and determines eligibility for the HVAC/R Unlimited Contractor category.

  1. Gain qualifying mechanical experience. Build and document verifiable experience in the mechanical trade.
  2. Meet journeyman-level qualifications. Oklahoma mechanical contractor applicants must first satisfy the applicable requirements associated with journeyman qualification.
  3. Complete the additional contractor experience requirement. Mechanical contractor applicants must meet the journeyman requirements plus an additional year of qualifying mechanical trade experience.
  4. Maintain the required relationship with the mechanical firm. A mechanical contractor must be a permanent employee, owner, partner, or officer of the mechanical firm.
  5. Submit the mechanical contractor application. Provide the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board with the required application and supporting experience documentation.
  6. Receive authorization for examination. The Board reviews eligibility before an applicant proceeds to testing.
  7. Schedule examinations through PSI. Approved applicants arrange their HVACR Contractor Unlimited and applicable Mechanical Business and Law examinations.
  8. Prepare with the exam references. Study HVACR theory, codes, calculations, duct design, refrigeration, heating, natural gas, electrical controls, and safety.
  9. Complete the required examinations. Achieve the required passing scores for the contractor licensing process.
  10. Address active contractor requirements. Complete applicable insurance, bond, and other requirements before operating under an active Oklahoma mechanical contractor license.

State Requirements

Oklahoma requires mechanical contractor applicants to meet the applicable journeyman qualifications plus an additional year of mechanical trade experience. Oklahoma defines one year of verifiable experience as 2,000 hours.

All mechanical contractors must also be a permanent employee, owner, partner, or officer in the mechanical firm associated with the contractor license.

The HVAC/R Unlimited Contractor license authorizes the contractor to install, alter, modify, service, maintain, or repair cooling products, systems, and equipment, including process piping; heating equipment, including process piping; sheet metal; natural gas piping; and refrigeration.

The Unlimited category is important for contractors performing HVAC work beyond the limitations of the HVAC/R Limited classification. Oklahoma identifies the Limited category as applying to cooling systems of no more than 25 tons and heating equipment with an input of no more than 500,000 Btu/h per appliance. Work beyond those limitations requires the applicable Unlimited HVAC/R license.

After satisfying examination requirements, contractors must also address the requirements necessary to maintain an active Oklahoma mechanical contractor license, including applicable bond and insurance obligations.

Oklahoma also recognizes qualifying mechanical education. Other approved education-and-experience combinations are available for qualifying vocational programs with fewer instructional hours.

  2. Review the qualifying pathways. Virginia recognizes different combinations of practical HVAC experience, formal vocational training, related education, apprenticeship completion, and other qualifying credentials.
  3. Document practical experience. Applicants must provide evidence supporting the HVAC experience required for the qualification pathway being used.
  4. Document training or education when applicable. Candidates using formal vocational training, technical education, apprenticeship, or related college education must provide the required supporting documentation.

  7. Prepare for the examination. Study HVAC trade knowledge, Virginia regulations, and the applicable references.

Virginia provides multiple qualification pathways for applicants seeking Journeyman HVAC licensure. These pathways use different combinations of practical trade experience and formal education or training.

One pathway includes four years of practical experience combined with 240 hours of formal vocational training. Additional pathways recognize five years of practical experience with 160 hours of formal vocational training, six years of practical experience with 80 hours of formal vocational training, or seven years of practical experience with 40 hours of formal vocational training.

Candidates with qualifying postsecondary education may use other pathways. An applicant with a related associate degree or certificate from an appropriate tradesman-related program may qualify with the applicable practical experience. Virginia regulations also recognize approved apprenticeship completion and other qualifying circumstances. Candidates should apply using the pathway that accurately reflects their education, training, apprenticeship, and practical HVAC experience.

Each component has a specific function, and a problem in one part of the system can affect every other part.

The compressor moves refrigerant through the system and raises the pressure of the refrigerant vapor. The condenser rejects heat and changes the refrigerant from vapor toward a liquid condition. The metering device controls refrigerant flow and creates the pressure reduction needed before the evaporator. The evaporator absorbs heat from the refrigerated space or product area.

Piping questions may address suction, discharge, and liquid lines. Exam Details

The Delaware Master HVACR Restricted – Refrigeration examination evaluates the knowledge associated with installing, maintaining, repairing, and altering refrigeration systems and related equipment. The restricted Refrigeration classification applies to systems used to cool a surface or area below 55 degrees Fahrenheit or 12.9 degrees Celsius for food and product preservation, without a tonnage limitation.

Preparation should include refrigeration theory, mechanical code requirements, system components, equipment installation, controls, piping, maintenance, service, safety, and troubleshooting. Candidates may need to apply practical field knowledge while also locating supporting information in the authorized references.

Important preparation areas include:

  • Basic refrigeration principles and the refrigeration cycle
  • Heat transfer, temperature, pressure, and system relationships
  • Compressors, condensers, evaporators, and metering devices
  • Refrigeration piping and system components
  • Mechanical equipment installation requirements
  • Equipment access, clearances, and service considerations
  • Motors, electrical controls, and safety devices
  • System charging and operating conditions
  • Commercial refrigeration equipment
  • Refrigerated spaces and product-preservation systems
  • System inspection and preventive maintenance
  • Troubleshooting and service procedures
  • Mechanical ventilation and equipment-room considerations
  • Workplace and refrigeration safety

Candidates should understand the refrigeration cycle and the function of the principal components. A refrigeration system depends on the relationship between the compressor, condenser, metering device, evaporator, refrigerant, piping, controls, and heat-transfer conditions. A change in one component or operating condition can affect the performance of the complete system.

Equipment questions may involve compressors, condensers, evaporators, receivers, accumulators, metering devices, valves, fans, motors, controls, and safety devices. Candidates should understand the purpose of each component, its position in the system, and the symptoms that may appear when it fails or operates incorrectly.

Mechanical-code preparation may address equipment installation, machinery rooms, ventilation, access, clearances, ducts, exhaust, appliances, system protection, and other requirements relevant to refrigeration work. Candidates should practice using code definitions and chapter organization rather than relying only on field terminology.

Maintenance and troubleshooting questions may involve temperature and pressure readings, airflow, refrigerant flow, dirty components, failed controls, restricted lines, improper charging, compressor concerns, and system operating symptoms. A strong preparation plan should include both system theory and practical diagnostic reasoning.

Licensing Steps

The Delaware Board of Plumbing, Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Examiners regulates Master HVACR and Master HVACR Restricted licenses. Applicants pursuing the restricted Refrigeration classification must complete the state licensing process and receive approval before taking the master examination.

  1. Select the correct classification. Apply for the Delaware Master HVACR Restricted license and choose Refrigeration as the specialty.
  2. Create or access a DELPROS account. Delaware professional licensing applications are submitted through the Delaware Professional Regulation Online Services system.
  3. Complete the application. Provide the requested personal, apprenticeship, employment, experience, examination, and licensing information.
  4. Gather supporting documentation. Required records may include apprenticeship credentials, a journeyperson certificate, employment verification, supervised experience documentation, and verification of licenses held in other jurisdictions.
  5. Submit records as directed. Certain documents may need to be completed or submitted by an employer, supervisor, apprenticeship program, school, or licensing authority.
  6. Complete any applicable equivalency requirement. Applicants without the qualifying apprenticeship credential may need to satisfy the apprenticeship bypass or equivalency requirement associated with the Refrigeration specialty.
  7. Receive Board approval to test. The Board reviews the completed application and supporting records before authorizing the applicant to take the master examination.
  8. Register with the testing provider. Follow the examination registration and scheduling instructions supplied after approval.
  9. Take the examination. Follow the current requirements for identification, authorized references, calculators, appointment procedures, and testing conduct.
  10. Complete remaining licensing requirements. The Board must receive the examination result and all required records before issuing the professional license.
  11. Establish the contracting business. Form the LLC or corporation, obtain the EIN, and complete the registrations and operational steps that apply to the company.

The qualification pathway depends on the applicant’s apprenticeship training, journeyperson credential, supervised experience, examination requirements, and supporting records. The Delaware Board determines whether an applicant’s training, experience, examinations, and supporting documentation satisfy the licensing requirements. Exam Details

The Delaware Master HVACR Restricted Air Conditioning examination is part of the professional licensing process overseen by the Delaware Board of Plumbing, Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Examiners. Candidates applying by examination must receive Board approval before registering with the approved testing provider.

The examination contains 95 questions, and candidates are allowed four hours to complete it. Candidates should develop a pacing strategy that leaves sufficient time for direct-answer questions, calculations, plan interpretation, reference searches, and final review.

The examination outline includes General Knowledge, Plan Reading, Systems and Sizing, Piping, Equipment, and Maintenance. Each area requires candidates to combine field experience with technical understanding and efficient use of the reference materials.

General Knowledge includes 22 questions. Candidates should review heat transfer, temperature, pressure, humidity, airflow, refrigeration principles, combustion, electrical fundamentals, tools, safety practices, insulation, system operation, and common HVACR terminology.

Plan Reading includes eight questions. Candidates may need to interpret mechanical symbols, equipment schedules, duct layouts, piping routes, load information, plan notes, dimensions, equipment locations, and system details.

Systems and Sizing includes 17 questions. Preparation should include residential and commercial load calculations, equipment selection, airflow requirements, duct sizing, capacity, building characteristics, outdoor and indoor design conditions, and system-performance considerations.

Piping includes 14 questions. Candidates should review fuel-gas piping, refrigerant piping, approved materials, joining procedures, regulators, valves, supports, pressure considerations, sizing methods, testing, and protection from physical damage.

Equipment includes 18 questions. Study should address air-conditioning systems, refrigeration equipment, heat pumps, compressors, condensers, evaporators, metering devices, air handlers, warm-air heating equipment, controls, motors, and safety devices.

Maintenance includes 16 questions. Candidates should understand inspection procedures, troubleshooting, system testing, refrigerant-side evaluation, electrical checks, airflow measurements, equipment cleaning, control verification, leak detection, and preventive maintenance.

State Requirements

Delaware requires professionals providing regulated HVACR services to hold the appropriate license unless a specific exemption applies. A license from another jurisdiction does not automatically authorize HVACR work in Delaware.

A Master HVACR Restricted license permits services only in the specialty identified on the license. Delaware restricted specialties include forced-air heating, ventilation and gas piping; hydronic heating and gas piping; commercial hood systems; refrigeration; air conditioning; and gas piping.

The restricted air-conditioning classification applies to work within the air-conditioning specialty. Contractors planning to provide services across multiple restricted specialties should pursue the unrestricted Master HVACR license.

The examination description addresses air-conditioning and refrigeration systems, piping vessels, warm-air heating, boilers, ventilation systems, duct systems, insulation, and related components within complete systems, without a horsepower or tonnage limitation.

A Master HVACR Restricted license does not automatically provide authority for plumbing work involving systems used to bring water into a building or remove liquid and water-carried waste. Separate plumbing authority may be required for that work.

Applicants should submit complete, accurate, and consistent documentation. Missing experience records, incomplete license verification, or conflicting information may delay Board review and examination authorization.

The Delaware Board determines whether an applicant qualifies for examination and licensure. The testing provider administers the examination but does not decide whether an applicant satisfies the state’s professional licensing requirements.

After passing the examination, candidates must complete all remaining licensing requirements before the license can be issued. Applicants should monitor DELPROS and their email for updates or requests for additional information.

Delaware HVACR licenses are subject to renewal, continuing education, and professional conduct requirements. A professional HVACR license is separate from the business registrations, tax accounts, insurance, and local approvals required to operate a company.

Water accounts for 8 questions. Candidates should understand water as the heat-transfer medium in hydronic systems, including temperature, pressure, expansion, circulation, system filling, and conditions that can affect equipment performance.

Testing and Inspection accounts for 4 questions. Study system testing, pressure testing, inspection procedures, verification of safe equipment operation, leak detection, and recognition of improper or unsafe installations.

Evaporators absorb heat from the conditioned or refrigerated space. Review airflow, coil condition, refrigerant distribution, frost, defrost, temperature relationships, and the effect of restricted airflow on system performance.

Metering devices regulate refrigerant flow into the evaporator. Candidates should understand their purpose and how refrigerant flow influences evaporator operation and system balance.

Prepare for the Washington HVAC/Refrigeration Master Electrician examination with a focused book package built around the electrical code, Washington electrical law, and administrative rules used for the state's 06A HVAC/Refrigeration specialty. This package includes the Revised Code of Washington (RCW) Chapter 19.28, Washington Administrative Code (WAC) Chapter 296-46B, and the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 Edition.

Washington identifies HVAC/Refrigeration as electrical specialty classification 06A. The HVAC/R Master Electrician credential is a specialty master certification for experienced electricians who already hold the corresponding Washington specialty electrician certificate and meet the state's master electrician eligibility requirements. The examination requires candidates to apply electrical code requirements to HVAC and refrigeration equipment while also understanding Washington-specific licensing rules, specialty limitations, and electrical regulations.

Washington electrical examinations are open book. Candidates may use approved reference materials during testing, making effective code navigation an important part of preparation. Candidates should become comfortable deciding whether an examination question is controlled by the NEC, RCW Chapter 19.28, or WAC Chapter 296-46B and locating the applicable provision efficiently.

The 06A HVAC/Refrigeration specialty covers defined electrical work associated with HVAC and refrigeration systems. Its scope includes specified telecommunications and Class 2 low-voltage control wiring, line-voltage components located within HVAC/refrigeration equipment, certain disconnecting means and controller components, limited raceway work for physical protection of low-voltage cables, qualifying flexible supply whips, and other work specifically authorized by Washington rules.

The Washington 06A specialty is not generally limited by voltage, phase, or amperage. However, the specialty remains limited to the HVAC/refrigeration scope established by Washington regulations. Master-level certification does not convert the 06A specialty into an unrestricted general electrical certification.

This book package combines the three primary references candidates need for an organized study approach. The NEC provides national electrical installation standards, RCW Chapter 19.28 establishes Washington electrical law, and WAC Chapter 296-46B defines the HVAC/Refrigeration specialty and contains detailed requirements governing certification, contractors, examinations, inspections, permits, and electrical installations.

What You Get

  • Revised Code of Washington (RCW) Chapter 19.28
    Washington's electrical law covering electricians, master electricians, electrical contractors, certification, installations, enforcement, responsibilities, and other statutory requirements governing electrical work in the state.
  • Washington Administrative Code (WAC) Chapter 296-46B
    Washington's detailed electrical safety, licensing, certification, examination, specialty-scope, contractor, permit, inspection, and installation rules. This reference defines the 06A HVAC/Refrigeration specialty and its authorized electrical work.
  • National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 Edition
    The NEC edition currently identified for Washington electrical examinations. It provides technical requirements for HVAC equipment, motors, controllers, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, conductors, electrical equipment, hazardous locations, and related installations.

These references work together during examination preparation. A technical HVAC/R electrical question may be answered through the NEC, while a question involving specialty authority, licensing, master electrician responsibilities, or contractor compliance may require the RCW or WAC.

Exam Details

The Washington 06A HVAC/Refrigeration Master Electrician examination is divided into two required sections: NEC & Theory and Washington Codes.

  • NEC & Theory: Approximately 50 questions
  • Time Allowed for NEC & Theory: 3 hours
  • Washington Codes: Approximately 20 questions
  • Time Allowed for Washington Codes: 1 hour
  • Total Questions: Approximately 70 questions across both sections
  • Total Testing Time: Approximately 4 hours across both sections
  • Passing Score: 70% or greater on each required examination section
  • Exam Type: Open book
  • Testing Provider: PSI
  • Primary Code Reference: National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 Edition

The published NEC & Theory examination outline includes approximately two questions from NEC Article 90, three from NEC Articles 100 through 110, two from wiring and protection, five from overcurrent protection, five from grounding and bonding, six from wiring methods, four from electrical equipment, eight from motors, HVAC equipment, generators and transformers, one from equipment over 600 volts, one from hazardous locations, one from special equipment, two from special conditions, and approximately ten questions involving general trade knowledge and electrical theory.

The Washington Codes section includes approximately 20 questions involving Washington laws and rules. Candidates should be familiar with specialty scope, certification, master electrician requirements, contractor responsibilities, examination rules, permits, inspections, and other Washington-specific provisions contained in RCW Chapter 19.28 and WAC Chapter 296-46B.

Open Book Test

The Washington HVAC/R Master Electrician examination is an open book test. Washington Labor & Industries permits approved reference materials in the testing center under established examination rules.

The 2020 National Electrical Code may be used. Permanent index tabs are permitted. Removable tabs, sticky notes, and handwritten notes are prohibited. Original copyrighted reference materials may contain highlighting, underlining, and permanent index tabs when they otherwise comply with examination rules.

Printed copies of RCW Chapter 19.28 and WAC Chapter 296-46B may also be brought into the examination. Printed copies of Washington electrical laws and rules must be prepared according to testing requirements, including placement in a three-ring binder.

Because the NEC & Theory section contains approximately 50 questions in three hours, candidates should develop efficient reference-navigation habits before test day. Topics involving motors, HVAC equipment, conductor sizing, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, disconnects, and wiring methods should become familiar areas of the NEC.

Washington-specific navigation is equally important. Questions involving the scope of the 06A specialty, master electrician authority, contractor assignments, permits, inspections, or certification requirements may require WAC Chapter 296-46B or RCW Chapter 19.28 instead of the NEC.

Licensing Steps

Washington HVAC/Refrigeration Master Electrician certification is administered through the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries. Candidates follow the specialty master electrician pathway.

  1. Hold a Washington 06A HVAC/Refrigeration Electrician certificate. The applicant must first be certified by Labor & Industries in the applicable specialty.
  2. Hold the specialty certificate for at least two years. Washington requires specialty Master Electrician applicants to have been certified in the applicable specialty for at least two years.
  3. Apply for the Master Electrician examination. Submit the applicable examination application through Washington Labor & Industries.
  4. Receive examination approval. L&I reviews the application and verifies that the candidate meets the qualification requirements.
  5. Prepare for NEC & Theory and Washington Codes. Study the NEC, RCW, and WAC with emphasis on HVAC/R electrical equipment, motors, controls, and Washington specialty rules.

Washington Master Electricians may work with the tools of the trade within the scope of their certification. A Master Electrician may also serve as the designated master electrician for an electrical contractor when the applicable contractor classification and assignment requirements are satisfied.

When a master electrician is assigned to an electrical contractor, the master electrician accepts responsibility for helping ensure that the contractor complies with Washington electrical laws and rules.

State Requirements

Washington identifies HVAC/Refrigeration as electrical specialty classification 06A. To qualify for the specialty Master Electrician examination, an applicant must have been certified by Washington Labor & Industries in the 06A specialty for at least two years.

The underlying 06A HVAC/Refrigeration Electrician certification requires 4,000 hours of qualifying work experience. Trainees working toward the 06A specialty must work under an appropriately certified specialty electrician or a general journey level electrician and must be supervised at least 75 percent of the time.

Washington also requires candidates in the 4,000-hour specialty pathway to complete 48 hours of basic classroom instruction before they can qualify for examination under the applicable pathway.

The 06A specialty is not limited by voltage, phase, or amperage, but its work must remain within the HVAC/refrigeration scope defined by Washington rules. Washington places additional supervision restrictions on trainees working on HVAC/refrigeration systems containing circuits rated over 600 volts.

The specialty may perform specified telecommunications and Class 2 low-voltage control wiring and component work associated with HVAC/refrigeration systems. Washington rules distinguish between residential occupancies and other occupancies when defining portions of this authority.

The 06A scope also permits installation, repair, replacement, and maintenance of line-voltage components located within HVAC/refrigeration equipment. This can include qualifying equipment accessories installed within and powered from the HVAC/refrigeration system.

The specialty may repair, replace, or maintain internal components of HVAC/refrigeration equipment disconnecting means or controllers when the work meets the limitations established by Washington rules.

Washington also permits the specialty to install short sections of raceway for physical protection of low-voltage cables and to perform qualifying repair, replacement, or maintenance involving line-voltage flexible supply whips when the work falls within the stated restrictions.

The 06A specialty does not provide unrestricted authority to install general line-voltage services, feeders, branch circuits, external controllers, or disconnect switches. WAC 296-46B establishes specific exceptions and limitations that candidates should study carefully.

The 06B specialty may not perform electrical work where the primary electrical power connection to the HVAC/refrigeration system exceeds 250 volts, single phase, or 120 amperes. This restriction is a defining feature of the classification and is an important subject for candidates to understand.

The specialty may install, repair, replace, and maintain specified HVAC/refrigeration telecommunications and Class 2 low-voltage control wiring and components in residential occupancies. It also permits qualifying HVAC/R telecommunications and Class 2 low-voltage control work in nonresidential occupancies that have no more than three stories on or above grade.

The classification may perform qualifying work on line-voltage components located within HVAC/refrigeration equipment. It may also repair, replace, or maintain internal components of qualifying equipment disconnecting means or controllers when the equipment meets the conditions established by Washington rules.

The 06B specialty may install short sections of raceway to provide physical protection for low-voltage cables. Washington defines limitations on this work so that the protective raceway does not become an unrestricted raceway installation between devices, junction boxes, or other components.

The specialty may also repair, replace, or maintain qualifying line-voltage flexible supply whips that are not more than six feet in length when the work meets the requirements of WAC Chapter 296-46B.

06B generally may not install line-voltage controllers or disconnect switches external to HVAC/refrigeration equipment. Washington rules provide a limited exception involving certain like-in-kind disconnecting means replacements associated with HVAC/R equipment replacement when all stated conditions are met.

Administrator certificates are renewed on a three-year cycle. Washington requires approved continuing education for renewal, including code-update and RCW/WAC content. An administrator assigned to an electrical contractor must also follow Washington requirements regarding changes in assignment status.

Administrator certification by itself does not authorize the certificate holder to perform electrical installation work or work with the tools of the electrical trade. Anyone personally performing electrical work must hold the appropriate Washington electrician certification and work within the applicable licensing requirements.

A specialty electrical administrator may only be assigned to an electrical contractor holding the corresponding specialty. A 07D Appliance Repair Administrator therefore provides administrative coverage for the matching Appliance Repair contractor specialty rather than unrestricted general electrical contracting authority.

The 07D specialty covers servicing, maintaining, repairing, or replacing household appliances, small commercial or industrial appliances, and other small electrical utilization equipment.

For purposes of the specialty, the appliance or electrical utilization equipment must be self-contained and built to standardized sizes or types. The equipment must connect as a single unit to a single source of electrical power limited to a maximum of 250 volts, 60 amperes, and single phase.

Examples of qualifying equipment can include ovens, office equipment, vehicle-repair equipment, commercial kitchen equipment, self-contained hot tubs and spas, grinders, scales, and other equipment that fits the Washington definition.

Washington excludes several types of systems and equipment from the Appliance Repair specialty. These include alarm and energy-management systems, similar integrated systems, luminaires, furnaces, heaters, air conditioners, heat pumps, sewage-disposal equipment, door and gate systems, and individual components installed together to create a larger system.

The specialty includes in-place like-in-kind replacement of qualifying appliances or equipment when the same unmodified electrical circuit is used to supply the replacement. It also includes like-in-kind replacement of electrical components located within the appliance or equipment.

The 07D scope permits disconnection and reconnection of low-voltage control wiring and line-voltage supply whips that are not more than six feet in length, provided the characteristics of the branch circuit are not modified.

Washington also allows installation of an outlet box and outlet at an existing appliance or equipment location when converting the appliance from a permanent electrical connection to a plug-and-cord connection. Other than the installation of that outlet box and outlet, the existing branch circuit supplying the appliance or equipment cannot be modified.

The specialty does not include installation, repair, or modification of branch-circuit conductors, services, feeders, panelboards, disconnect switches, or raceway and conductor systems that interconnect multiple appliances, pieces of equipment, or other electrical components.

The 07D specialty also does not authorize electrical work in classified hazardous locations governed by the NEC provisions excluded by Washington rules. Plumbing work regulated under Washington plumbing law is likewise outside the electrical specialty.

These limits are especially important for an administrator because an assigned administrator accepts responsibility for helping ensure that the electrical contractor performs work within the scope of its license and follows applicable Washington electrical laws and rules.

    This reference contains Washington electrical statutes governing administrators, contractors, electricians, certification, electrical installations, enforcement, and legal responsibilities within the state's electrical licensing system.

    This reference contains Washington rules governing administrator certification, contractor requirements, specialty classifications, examinations, permits, inspections, assignments, and the detailed scope of 07D Appliance Repair work.
  • National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 Edition

Overcurrent Protection: Study breakers, fuses, equipment ratings, conductor protection, and branch-circuit protection. Understand how the existing branch circuit relates to replacement appliances and equipment.

Grounding and Bonding: Review equipment grounding conductors, bonding, grounding continuity, enclosures, flexible connections, and grounding requirements associated with appliance and utilization equipment.

Wiring Methods: Study cables, raceways, boxes, fittings, conductor protection, and flexible wiring methods. Candidates should understand the technical rules even though the 07D specialty sharply limits modifications to branch circuits and raceway systems.

Special Conditions: Review NEC provisions involving special electrical conditions identified in the published examination outline.

Washington electrical administrator certification is administered through the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries. Administrator candidates follow a different examination pathway from electricians and Master Electricians because there are no experience prerequisites and no prior L&I examination approval requirement.

The scope includes like-in-kind replacement of qualifying utilization equipment when the same unmodified electrical circuit is used to supply the replacement equipment.

The specialty also includes like-in-kind replacement or repair of remote-control components that are integral to the operation of qualifying utilization equipment, as well as like-in-kind replacement or repair of electrical components within the equipment.

Virginia establishes specific experience standards for applicants seeking licensure as a master in a trade. A Master HVAC applicant must furnish evidence that one of the accepted experience standards has been met.

Current Virginia regulations provide three pathways for a master-level applicant:

  • Hold a valid Residential HVAC Tradesman license in the trade for three years;
  • Hold a valid Journeyman license in the trade for a minimum of one year; or
  • Document nine years of practical experience in the trade for which the master license is sought.

These requirements reflect the advanced level of experience expected from a Virginia Master HVAC tradesman. The examination is designed to test knowledge beyond basic equipment identification. Candidates should be prepared to work with heating and cooling principles, system installation requirements, ventilation, ductwork, combustion, refrigeration, controls, boilers, piping, commercial kitchen ventilation, and professional regulations.

Virginia Master HVAC tradesman licenses expire three years from the last day of the month in which the license was issued. As a condition of renewal, HVAC tradesmen must complete three hours of Board-approved continuing education related to applicable building code changes during the renewal period.

The continuing education requirement applies to both journeyman and master HVAC tradesmen. An individual holding both journeyman and master designations in the same trade does not have to duplicate the HVAC continuing education course solely because both designations are held.

Reference Books

  • Virginia Board for Contractors Individual License and Certification Regulations
    The regulatory reference used for Virginia tradesman examinations. It covers licensing definitions, qualifications, standards of practice, standards of conduct, renewal, reinstatement, and other requirements affecting licensed tradesmen.
  • Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition
    A technical HVAC reference identified in the current PSI examination materials. It covers refrigeration, air conditioning, heating systems, system components, service principles, controls, and related HVAC trade knowledge.

Candidates should study not only the technical material but also how the authorized references are organized. Knowing where major subjects are located can save valuable time during an open-book exam.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Virginia Master HVAC exam covers both broad HVAC theory and practical installation knowledge. Candidates should be comfortable identifying system components, understanding equipment operation, interpreting system requirements, and applying trade principles to common installation and service situations.

Warm air heating is an important exam area. Study furnace operation, heating components, airflow principles, equipment installation, controls, venting, and related safety considerations. Understand how the parts of a forced-air heating system interact rather than memorizing isolated definitions.

Ventilation and air conditioning systems are also major areas of the examination. Candidates should review ventilation concepts, exhaust requirements, air movement, cooling principles, system components, and common HVAC installation practices.

Duct systems require familiarity with airflow distribution, duct construction concepts, installation practices, insulation, and related system considerations. Flash cards can be useful for reinforcing terms and components while reference-book practice can strengthen your ability to locate detailed requirements.

Chimneys, flues, vents, and combustion air require careful study because improper installation can create serious operating and safety problems. Candidates should understand the purpose of these systems and the relationship between appliance operation, combustion, venting, and air supply.

Boilers and hot water piping are included on the Master HVAC examination. Review hydronic heating concepts, boiler system components, water circulation, piping arrangements, safety controls, and other principles associated with hot-water heating systems.

Controls and low-voltage systems are another part of the exam outline. HVAC professionals should understand basic control sequences, thermostatic control, low-voltage components, and how controls affect heating and cooling system operation.

Refrigerants and refrigerant piping require understanding of refrigeration principles and system operation. Study how refrigerant moves through a system, the function of major refrigeration components, and concepts associated with refrigerant piping and system performance.

The examination also includes fuel oil piping and storage, insulation, commercial kitchen venting, chilled and condenser water piping, and firestopping and penetration inspection. These subjects reinforce why Master-level exam preparation should cover the full outline rather than concentrating only on residential air conditioning.

A useful study method is to divide the 250 cards into manageable groups. Review one group until you can answer most cards confidently, then move to another group while continuing to revisit missed material. This creates spaced repetition and keeps difficult subjects in your study rotation.

When a flash card identifies a weak subject, open the applicable reference and study that topic in context. Locate the chapter or section where related information appears. Over time, this connects recall with reference navigation, which is especially valuable for a timed open-book examination.

You can also practice with a timer. Choose a subject, locate a related rule or technical concept in your reference material, and note how quickly you can find it. The objective is not to memorize an entire technical book. The objective is to understand enough about the subject to know where to look and how to confirm an answer efficiently.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps candidates approach the Virginia Master HVAC exam with a more organized study structure. Instead of treating the examination as one large collection of technical information, these 250 flash cards allow you to break preparation into shorter, focused review sessions.

Trade-focused flash-card review can help reinforce heating principles, air conditioning systems, ventilation, ductwork, boilers, combustion air, controls, refrigeration, piping, and professional regulations. Repeated exposure helps make terminology and concepts easier to recognize when you encounter them in an exam question.

For an open-book examination, preparation should also include reference navigation. 1 Exam Prep encourages candidates to combine knowledge review with practice locating information. When you understand a subject well enough to recognize it quickly, you have a better starting point for finding the supporting section in an authorized reference.

The study structure is designed to build familiarity and confidence through consistent preparation. Review the cards, identify weaker subjects, return to the applicable material, and continue practicing until the exam outline feels more manageable. This approach supports a disciplined preparation process without promising a particular examination or licensing outcome.

FAQ Section

How many flash cards are included?

This study product includes 250 Virginia Master HVAC exam prep flash cards.

Is the Virginia Master HVAC exam open book?

Yes. The Virginia Master HVAC examination is open book. Candidates must follow PSI rules regarding authorized references, permanent tabs, notes, and materials allowed in the examination center.

How many questions are on the Virginia Master HVAC exam?

The Journeyman/Master HVAC examination contains 85 items. A Master HVAC candidate must answer at least 64 items correctly to achieve the required Master passing score.

How much time is allowed for the Virginia Master HVAC exam?

Candidates receive 210 minutes to complete the Virginia Journeyman/Master HVAC examination.

Who administers the Virginia Master HVAC exam?

PSI administers the examination for the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation and the Virginia Board for Contractors.

Do I need approval before scheduling the exam?

Yes. Virginia requires Board pre-approval before a tradesman candidate may sit for the examination.

What subjects should I study for the Master HVAC exam?

The exam covers Virginia licensing regulations and technical subjects including warm air heating, ventilation, air conditioning, ducts, boilers, hot water piping, combustion air, controls, oil systems, commercial kitchen venting, refrigerants, refrigerant piping, chilled and condenser water piping, and firestopping.

Can I use removable tabs in my exam books?

No. PSI permits permanent tabs but does not allow removable tabs in examination references. Reference materials must comply with the examination provider's rules.

Do these flash cards replace the reference books?

No. The flash cards are supplemental exam-preparation materials. Candidates should also study the applicable authorized references and practice locating information within them.

What experience is required to become a Virginia Master HVAC tradesman?

Virginia provides multiple qualification pathways, including three years holding a valid Residential HVAC Tradesman license, at least one year holding a valid journeyman license in the trade, or nine years of practical experience in the trade.

Does a Virginia Master HVAC license require continuing education?

Yes. HVAC tradesmen must complete three hours of Board-approved continuing education related to applicable building code changes as a condition of renewal.

How should I use the 250 study flash cards?

Study the cards in smaller groups, mark subjects that require additional attention, and repeatedly review weaker areas. Pair the flash cards with reference-book navigation so you practice both knowledge recall and finding information efficiently during an open-book exam.

  • Standards of Practice
  • Standards of Conduct
  • Renewal and Reinstatement

A stronger approach combines HVAC knowledge with selective reference use. Licensing Steps

The Virginia Residential HVAC Tradesman credential is issued to individuals through the Virginia Board for Contractors. Pre-approval from the Board is required before candidates can schedule the examination.

  1. Review the Residential HVAC eligibility requirements. Virginia provides several qualification pathways based on practical experience and formal vocational training.
  2. Choose the applicable qualification pathway. Determine which combination of HVAC experience and vocational education applies to your background.
  3. Document practical trade experience. Applicants using an experience pathway must provide the required experience verification.
  4. Provide training documentation when applicable. Applicants using vocational education to meet the qualification requirement must submit appropriate certificates or transcripts.
  5. Submit the Residential Tradesman Exam and License Application. Select Residential Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning Tradesman as the requested designation.
  6. Receive Board approval. Examination approval is required before scheduling through PSI.
  7. Prepare for the examination. Review the Virginia regulations, mechanical code, HVAC technical material, and residential load calculations.
  8. Schedule and complete the PSI examination. Once approved, candidates can proceed with examination registration.
  9. Complete the licensing process. After satisfying the applicable requirements, the individual can proceed toward issuance of the Residential HVAC Tradesman credential.

The Residential HVAC Tradesman license is an individual license and should not be confused with a Virginia contractor business license. A business performing contracting work that requires contractor licensure must satisfy the applicable contractor business requirements separately.

State Requirements

Virginia's Residential HVAC Tradesman pathway became available as an additional licensing option for individuals working in residential HVAC. The credential is limited to residential structures, and commercial HVAC work is not permitted under the residential license.

Applicants must be at least 18 years old and satisfy one of the state's approved qualification pathways. Current Virginia qualification options include:

  • Two years of practical experience plus 160 hours of formal vocational training.
  • Three years of practical experience plus 120 hours of formal vocational training.
  • Four years of practical experience plus 80 hours of formal vocational training.
  • Five years of practical experience plus 40 hours of formal vocational training.
  • Six or more years of practical experience in the trade.

Applicants qualifying through practical experience must provide the required experience verification. Candidates relying on formal vocational education must provide appropriate documentation of that training.

Virginia also provides a pathway for certain applicants who currently hold a residential tradesman license or certification issued by another governing body. Supporting licensing documentation must be provided when using that qualification pathway.

The Residential HVAC Tradesman credential is separate from journeyman and master HVAC licensing. Residential HVAC experience can also form part of a future pathway toward higher tradesman credentials when the applicable Virginia experience and licensing requirements are met.

Exam Details

The Kentucky Journeyman HVAC Mechanic examination is administered through the International Code Council (ICC) contractor and trades examination program. It evaluates knowledge of HVAC installation practices, mechanical codes, safety principles, equipment operation, and technical requirements.

  • Exam Name: Kentucky Journeyman HVAC
  • Exam Code: 598-KY
  • Exam Organization: International Code Council (ICC)
  • Testing Provider: Pearson VUE
  • Exam Format: Computer-based, multiple-choice examination
  • Number of Questions: 60
  • Time Limit: 3 hours
  • Exam Type: Open book
  • Online Practice Access: 3 months

The ICC examination outline divides the Kentucky Journeyman HVAC examination into five major subject areas:

  • HVAC Principles, Terminology, Administration, and Safety – 23%: Fundamental HVAC concepts, industry terminology, mechanical requirements, and safety practices.
  • HVAC Installation Requirements – 15%: Installation principles, equipment requirements, and relevant mechanical code provisions.
  • Venting, Combustion Air, and Gas Piping – 21%: Fuel gas systems, combustion air requirements, venting principles, and piping-related considerations.
  • Boilers, Duct, Electrical, and Exhaust – 21%: Heating equipment, duct systems, electrical concepts, and mechanical exhaust requirements.
  • Plan Analysis – 20%: Understanding and interpreting information presented in mechanical plans and construction documents.

These examination categories provide a useful framework for organizing your study sessions. Because the test covers several areas of HVAC knowledge, successful preparation requires attention to both technical principles and the application of mechanical code requirements.

Plan analysis, safety, and installation topics are especially important for candidates who are accustomed to hands-on fieldwork but have less experience answering code-based examination questions.

Test Information and Study Materials

General Electrical Knowledge

General electrical knowledge provides the foundation for understanding HVAC equipment wiring. Review common electrical terms, circuit components, electrical quantities, and the functions of protective devices.

Electrical Theory

Electrical theory explains how current flows through circuits and how electrical equipment uses power. Study voltage, resistance, current, and the relationship between electrical supply and equipment operation.

Ohm's Law

Ohm's Law describes the mathematical relationship between voltage, current, and resistance. Practice identifying known quantities and using the appropriate calculation to solve electrical problems.

Electrical Power Calculations

Electrical power calculations are useful when evaluating equipment loads. Review watts, volts, amperes, and the relationships used to describe electrical power.

Basic Load Calculations

Load calculations help determine the electrical demand associated with connected equipment. Study how equipment ratings and electrical characteristics affect circuit requirements.

Electrical Definitions

The NEC defines terms used throughout electrical installation requirements. Review definitions associated with conductors, circuits, equipment, disconnecting means, grounding, and accessibility.

Feeders and Branch Circuits

Feeders and branch circuits distribute power through electrical systems. Review general circuit arrangements, conductor requirements, and the relationship between supply circuits and connected HVAC equipment.

Conductor Selection

Conductors must be selected for their intended use. Study conductor materials, insulation ratings, ampacity, and environmental conditions affecting electrical installations.

Conductor Ampacity

Ampacity describes the current a conductor can carry under specified conditions. Practice using NEC conductor tables and recognizing the installation factors that influence conductor selection.

Overcurrent Protection

Overcurrent protective devices help protect conductors and equipment against excessive current. Review circuit breakers, fuses, protective ratings, and applicable NEC requirements.

Wiring Methods

Wiring methods provide pathways and protection for electrical conductors. Study raceways, cables, fittings, boxes, and installation requirements that apply to HVAC equipment connections.

Equipment Disconnects

Disconnecting means allow electrical equipment to be isolated from its supply. Review the purpose of HVAC equipment disconnects and the importance of understanding the authorized LM-H work boundary.

Thermostat Wiring

Thermostats are commonly used to control heating and cooling equipment. Study basic thermostat circuit functions, control wiring terminology, and the electrical relationships between thermostats and HVAC equipment.

Control Circuits

Control circuits regulate equipment operation. Review basic control functions involving switches, relays, contactors, and other devices used in HVAC systems.

Low-Voltage Controls

Many HVAC systems use low-voltage control wiring. Study the role of control transformers, low-voltage circuits, and equipment control components.

Transformers

Transformers change voltage levels to supply appropriate electrical power for specific components. Review transformer fundamentals and their role in HVAC control systems.

Equipment Grounding

Equipment grounding helps establish a fault-current path for electrical safety. Study equipment grounding conductors and the relevant requirements in NEC Article 250.

Bonding

Bonding connects conductive components to establish electrical continuity. Review bonding principles and their importance in equipment installations.

HVAC Equipment

Heating and cooling systems contain electrical components that control equipment operation. Review the relationship between power supplies, motors, controls, protective devices, and associated wiring.

Air-Conditioning Equipment

Air-conditioning systems use electrical power for compressors, fans, and other components. Study the electrical provisions in NEC Article 440 and their application to relevant equipment.

Refrigeration Equipment

Refrigeration equipment also uses motors and electrical controls. Review circuit protection, equipment ratings, conductor requirements, and applicable electrical installation principles.

HVAC Motor Fundamentals

Electric motors operate compressors, blowers, and fans. Review motor ratings, circuit requirements, controls, and the purpose of electrical protective equipment.

Motor Circuit Protection

Motor circuits require appropriate protective devices. Study the distinction between circuit protection and motor overload protection, together with their applicable NEC provisions.

Motor Controllers

Motor controllers regulate equipment operation. Review contactors, switches, and related control arrangements found in HVAC electrical systems.

Motor Disconnecting Means

Motor disconnecting means support equipment isolation. Study the general requirements for disconnects and their relationship to motor installations.

NEC Article 430

Article 430 contains requirements for motors, motor circuits, and controllers. Review its organization and the sections addressing conductor selection, protection, and motor equipment.

NEC Article 440

Article 440 addresses air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment. This article is especially useful for understanding electrical requirements affecting HVAC compressors and related equipment.

Equipment Nameplates

Electrical equipment nameplates provide important rating information. Practice recognizing voltage, current, and other electrical data used when evaluating equipment requirements.

Electrical Equipment Installation

Proper equipment installation involves suitable conductors, protective devices, disconnecting means, and wiring methods. Review how these components work together in an HVAC electrical installation.

Electrical Safety Practices

HVAC electrical work involves hazards associated with energized circuits and operating machinery. Review safe isolation, protective devices, grounding, and the importance of established electrical safety procedures.

NEC Reference Navigation

Practice using the 2023 NEC table of contents, index, definitions, article headings, and technical tables. Focus on locating requirements involving conductors, motors, controls, and air-conditioning equipment.

Using Ugly's Electrical References

Florida Class A Air Conditioning Contractor

A Class B Air Conditioning Contractor works within a more limited system-capacity classification. Florida defines the Class B scope as systems involving no more than 25 tons of cooling and 500,000 BTU of heating in any one system.

Class B contractors may perform qualifying installation, repair, maintenance, alteration, and related HVAC activities within their authorized scope.

Neither classification automatically authorizes work outside its statutory definition, including certain plumbing, fuel-line, and electrical power wiring activities.

Florida certified contractor applicants generally must demonstrate qualifying experience or an accepted combination of education and experience. The applicable licensing application establishes the documentation and qualifications required for the selected classification.
